chem_edx.7.0.summary: This core practical investigates how changing a condition (such as **concentration, temperature or surface area**) affects the **rate of reaction**. Edexcel names two methods: **measuring the production of a gas** in the reaction between hydrochloric acid and marble chips, and **observing a colour change** (the cloudiness from sulfur) in the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid. You must be able to describe each method, identify the independent, dependent and control variables, process results (including mean rate and 1/time) and evaluate errors and improvements.

core.h: What the core practical asks you to do
core.p: The specification requires you to investigate the effects of changing the conditions of a reaction on the rate of a chemical reaction by **(a) measuring the production of a gas** (in the reaction between **hydrochloric acid and marble chips**) and **(b) observing a colour change** (in the reaction between **sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid**). In both cases you change one condition, keep everything else the same, and measure how quickly the reaction goes.
bullets: **Rate of reaction** is how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed
Conditions that can be changed: **concentration** of a solution, **temperature**, **surface area** (size of solid pieces)
Method (a) measures **volume of gas produced** (or **loss in mass**) over time
Method (b) measures the **time taken** for a cross to disappear as the mixture turns cloudy
A **fair test** changes only one variable at a time

callouts.p: Rate of reaction = amount of reactant used or amount of product formed divided by the time taken.

core.h: Reaction 1: marble chips and hydrochloric acid
core.p: Marble is mainly **calcium carbonate**. It reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce calcium chloride, water and **carbon dioxide gas**. The rate can be followed by collecting and measuring the carbon dioxide or by measuring the mass lost as the gas escapes.
bullets: Word equation: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
Symbol equation: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
Observations: **fizzing / effervescence**, marble chips get smaller
The faster the gas is produced, the faster the reaction
Conditions usually changed: **surface area** (large chips, small chips, powder), **concentration** of acid, or temperature

callouts.p: The gas is carbon dioxide. It could be confirmed with limewater, which turns milky (cloudy).

core.h: Method (a): measuring the volume of gas
core.p: The carbon dioxide is collected in a **gas syringe** (or an upturned measuring cylinder full of water) and its volume read at regular time intervals. The experiment is then repeated with a different chip size or acid concentration.
bullets: Measure a fixed volume of hydrochloric acid (for example 50 cm3) with a **measuring cylinder** and pour it into a **conical flask**
Weigh a fixed mass of marble chips of one size (for example 5.0 g)
Add the chips, **immediately insert the bung** connected to the gas syringe, and **start the stop clock**
Record the **volume of gas** every 10 or 30 seconds until no more gas is produced
Repeat with **smaller chips or powder** (same mass), or with a **different concentration** of acid (same volume)
Repeat each experiment and calculate a **mean** for each condition
Alternative: collect gas by **displacement of water** in an upturned measuring cylinder; CO2 is slightly soluble in water so a gas syringe is more accurate

callouts.p: Gas produced before the bung is inserted is lost, so the measured volume is too low. Some students put the chips in a small tube inside the flask and tip it over after the bung is in.

core.h: Method (a) alternative: measuring loss in mass
core.p: Instead of collecting the gas, the flask can be placed on a **top-pan balance** with a loose **cotton wool plug** in the neck. The carbon dioxide escapes through the cotton wool, so the **mass decreases** over time. The cotton wool lets gas out but stops acid spray escaping, which would make the mass loss too large.
bullets: Place flask, acid and cotton wool on the balance; add the chips and start the clock
Record the **mass** at regular intervals until it stops changing
**Mass lost = mass of carbon dioxide** given off
Works well because CO2 is a fairly dense gas (relative formula mass 44), so the mass change is measurable
Plot **loss in mass** (or mass) against time

callouts.p: It allows carbon dioxide to escape but prevents droplets of acid being lost. It is not there to stop gas escaping.

core.h: Reaction 2: sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid
core.p: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium thiosulfate solution, a fine **precipitate of sulfur** forms. Sulfur is a pale yellow solid that does not dissolve, so the colourless solution gradually turns **cloudy (opaque) yellow**. The faster the reaction, the sooner the mixture becomes too cloudy to see through.
bullets: Word equation: sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + sulfur + sulfur dioxide + water
Symbol equation: Na2S2O3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + S(s) + SO2(g) + H2O(l)
The **sulfur precipitate** causes the cloudiness
**Sulfur dioxide** is a toxic gas that irritates the lungs, so the room must be well ventilated
Conditions usually changed: **temperature** of the thiosulfate solution, or **concentration** of sodium thiosulfate

callouts.p: Sulfur dioxide can trigger asthma attacks. Use small volumes, ventilate the room and pour finished mixtures into a container in a fume cupboard (or dispose of them promptly) rather than leaving them on the bench.

core.p: A cross is drawn on a piece of paper and a conical flask is placed on top. The time taken for the cross to **disappear from view** (when looking down through the solution from above) is measured. A shorter time means a faster rate.
bullets: Draw a **black cross** on a piece of white paper and place a conical flask on it
Measure a fixed volume of sodium thiosulfate solution (for example 50 cm3) into the flask
For temperature: warm the thiosulfate to the chosen temperature in a **water bath** and record the temperature with a **thermometer**
Add a fixed volume of hydrochloric acid (for example 5 cm3), swirl, and **start the stop clock**
**Look down** through the mixture from above and stop the clock when the cross can **no longer be seen**
Repeat at different temperatures (for example 20, 30, 40, 50 °C) or with different concentrations of thiosulfate (diluting with water but keeping the **total volume the same**)
Use the **same person** and the **same cross** each time, because judging when the cross disappears is subjective

callouts.p: When diluting the thiosulfate, make up to the same total volume with water (e.g. 40 cm3 thiosulfate + 10 cm3 water), so the depth of liquid the observer looks through stays the same.

fig.cap: The disappearing cross method. The observer looks down through the flask at a cross on paper; as yellow sulfur forms the mixture turns cloudy, and the clock is stopped when the cross can no longer be seen.

core.p: For any rate investigation you must be able to identify the variables. The **independent variable** is the one you change, the **dependent variable** is the one you measure, and the **control variables** are kept the same to make it a fair test.
bullets: Only change **one** independent variable at a time
Control variables must be **named specifically** (for example 'volume of acid', not just 'amount')
Temperature must be controlled even when it is not the independent variable, since it strongly affects rate

Independent variable
Dependent variable
Control variables
rows: Size of marble chips (large, small, powder)
Volume of CO2 at time intervals (or loss in mass)

Volume of CO2 at time intervals (or loss in mass)
Mass and size of marble chips, volume of acid, temperature
Volumes and concentrations of both solutions, same cross and flask
Total volume, volume and concentration of acid, temperature, same cross

callouts.p: A variable that is kept the same throughout an investigation so that it does not affect the results.

core.p: Results must be turned into a **rate** so that different conditions can be compared. For gas collection, the **mean rate** is the total volume of gas divided by the time taken. For the disappearing cross, the same amount of sulfur is needed to hide the cross each time, so **rate is proportional to 1/time**.
bullets: **Mean rate of reaction = amount of product formed ÷ time taken**
Gas volume: units **cm3/s**; mass loss: units **g/s**
Disappearing cross: **rate = 1 ÷ time**, units **1/s (s-1)**
Longer time → slower rate; shorter time → faster rate
Rate at a particular moment (Higher) is found from the **gradient of a tangent** to the curve on a graph
Calculate a **mean** of repeat results, leaving out any **anomalous** results

head: Temperature / °C
Time for cross to disappear / s
1/time / s-1

callouts.p: Always give units with a rate: cm3/s, g/s or s-1. A mark is often given for the unit.

core.p: For gas collection, plot **volume of gas (y-axis) against time (x-axis)**. The curve is **steepest at the start**, when the concentration of reactants is highest, then gets less steep and finally becomes **horizontal** when the reaction has finished. A **steeper** curve means a **faster** rate.
bullets: Powder or more concentrated acid gives a **steeper initial gradient**
The line levels off sooner when the rate is faster
If the same amounts of reactant are used, the **final volume is the same**, because the same amount of product forms
If a reactant (for example acid) is doubled in amount, the final volume increases
For the disappearing cross, plot **1/time (or time) against temperature or concentration**; draw a smooth curve or line of best fit

callouts.p: Steeper gradient = faster rate. Horizontal line = reaction has stopped because a reactant has been used up.

core.p: In both practicals, increasing concentration, temperature or surface area **increases the rate of reaction**. You should be able to state the conclusion in terms of the measured data and briefly link it to collision theory, which is covered in detail in the next spec points.
bullets: **Smaller chips / powder** → larger surface area → gas produced faster (steeper curve)
**More concentrated acid** → gas produced faster
**Higher temperature** → cross disappears in **less time** → faster rate
**More concentrated thiosulfate** → cross disappears in less time
Link: more frequent (and, for temperature, more energetic) collisions between reacting particles
For temperature, a rise of 10 °C roughly halves the time in this experiment, so the rate roughly doubles

callouts.p: 'Describe' questions want the pattern from the data (as temperature increases the time decreases). 'Explain' questions also want the reason (particles collide more frequently with more energy).

core.p: Examiners often ask you to evaluate these methods. Know the main sources of error for each and how they could be reduced.
bullets: Gas lost **before the bung is inserted** → volume too low; use a divided flask or tip in a small tube after sealing
**Gas syringe plunger sticking** → readings jump; tap or use a well-lubricated syringe
Collecting over water: **CO2 dissolves slightly** in water → use a gas syringe instead
Marble chips are **not all exactly the same size**, so the surface area varies
Disappearing cross: judging when the cross disappears is **subjective** → same person, same cross, same lighting, or use a **light sensor / data logger**
Temperature of the mixture **falls** after removing from the water bath → measure the temperature of the mixture, or keep the flask in the water bath
**Reaction time** in starting and stopping the clock → repeat and calculate a mean
Use a **burette or pipette** instead of a measuring cylinder for more accurate volumes

callouts.p: 'Be more careful' or 'do it again' earns nothing. Say exactly what to change and why, e.g. 'use a light sensor so that the end point is not judged by eye'.

core.p: A risk assessment identifies the hazards and how to reduce them. These points are commonly asked for 1 or 2 marks.
bullets: Wear **eye protection** (dilute acid is an irritant to eyes)
Hydrochloric acid at higher concentrations is **corrosive**; wipe up spills and wash skin with water
**Sulfur dioxide** is toxic: use a well-ventilated room, small volumes, and dispose of mixtures quickly or in a fume cupboard; anyone with **asthma** should take extra care
Do not heat thiosulfate solutions above about 50 °C, as more sulfur dioxide is released
Take care with hot water baths to avoid scalds
Handle glass syringes carefully; do not let the plunger fly out by using too much reactant

analogy.t: Timing a race with two stopwatches
analogy.p: Measuring rate is like timing runners. Method (a) is like watching a runner and writing down how far they have gone every 10 seconds: you get a full picture of how their speed changes (fast at the start, slowing down as they tire, then stopping). Method (b) is like only timing how long each runner takes to reach a fixed finish line: you do not see the speed during the race, but a shorter time still means a faster runner, and 1/time gives a number that goes up when they go faster. Where it breaks down: a reaction slows down because reactant particles are being used up, not because it gets tired, and in the cross experiment the 'finish line' is judged by eye, so it is less precise than a real finish line.

terms.d: How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed; amount of product formed or reactant used divided by time.
The total amount of product formed (or reactant used) divided by the total time taken.
The variable that is deliberately changed in an investigation.
The variable that is measured to see the effect of changing the independent variable.
A variable kept the same so that it does not affect the results, making the test fair.
An investigation in which only the independent variable is changed and all other variables are kept the same.
A piece of apparatus with a moving plunger and scale used to collect and measure the volume of a gas.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react; in this practical, sulfur.
Fizzing caused by bubbles of gas being produced in a liquid.
The total area of a solid exposed to the other reactant; smaller pieces have a larger surface area for the same mass.
The amount of a substance dissolved in a given volume of solution, for example in g/dm3 or mol/dm3.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results and is left out when calculating a mean.
Results are repeatable if the same person using the same method and equipment gets similar results.
Results are reproducible if a different person, or a different method or equipment, gives similar results.
The steepness of a line on a graph; on a product-time graph a steeper gradient means a faster rate.
A straight line touching a curve at one point, used (Higher) to find the rate at a particular time from its gradient.

mistakes.w: The cotton wool stops the gas escaping.
mistakes.r: The cotton wool lets the carbon dioxide escape but stops acid spray being lost.

mistakes.w: The cross disappears because the solution changes colour to yellow.
mistakes.r: A precipitate of (insoluble) sulfur forms, making the mixture cloudy / opaque so the cross cannot be seen.

mistakes.w: A longer time means a faster reaction.
mistakes.r: A longer time means a slower reaction; rate is proportional to 1/time.

mistakes.w: Control variable: the amount of chemicals.
mistakes.r: Name it precisely: the volume of hydrochloric acid, the mass of marble chips, the concentration of acid.

mistakes.w: The gas produced is hydrogen (it pops).
mistakes.r: Carbonates and acid produce carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

mistakes.w: Powdered marble gives more gas.
mistakes.r: Powder gives gas faster (steeper curve), but the same mass of marble with the same acid gives the same final volume.

mistakes.w: Improve the experiment by being more accurate.
mistakes.r: Give a specific improvement, e.g. use a gas syringe instead of collecting over water, or use a light sensor instead of judging the cross by eye.

mistakes.w: Rate units: seconds.
mistakes.r: Rate units are cm3/s, g/s or s-1 (1/time); seconds is a unit of time.

mistakes.w: Increasing the concentration of thiosulfate by adding more thiosulfate solution.
mistakes.r: Keep the total volume constant by diluting with water, otherwise the depth of liquid changes too.

exam.q: Name the gas produced when marble chips react with hydrochloric acid.
model: Carbon dioxide / CO2
exam.tip: Marble is calcium carbonate: carbonate + acid gives CO2.

exam.q: Name the piece of apparatus that could be used to measure the volume of gas produced.
model: Gas syringe (accept upturned measuring cylinder / burette over water)
exam.tip: Spell out 'gas syringe', not just 'syringe'.

exam.q: Explain why a loose cotton wool plug is placed in the neck of the flask when measuring loss in mass.
model: Allows carbon dioxide / gas to escape
Stops acid (spray / liquid) escaping, which would affect the mass
exam.tip: Two jobs, two marks.

exam.q: Give the independent variable and two control variables in an experiment to find the effect of chip size on the rate of reaction between marble and hydrochloric acid.
model: Independent: size of marble chips / surface area
Control: mass of marble chips
Control: volume / concentration of acid / temperature (any one)
exam.tip: Control variables must be specific quantities.

exam.q: In the disappearing cross experiment, explain why the mixture becomes cloudy.
model: Sulfur is produced
It is an insoluble solid / precipitate
exam.tip: Mention both 'sulfur' and 'precipitate' or 'insoluble'.

exam.q: A student collected 48 cm3 of carbon dioxide in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.
exam.tip: Give the unit: cm3/s.

exam.q: The cross disappeared after 25 s at 40 °C. Calculate the rate of reaction as 1/time.
exam.tip: 1/time gives a bigger number for a faster reaction.

exam.q: Describe how the student could make sure the disappearing cross experiment is a fair test when investigating temperature.
model: Same volume and concentration of sodium thiosulfate
Same volume and concentration of hydrochloric acid
Same cross / same flask / same person judging
exam.tip: Fair test = everything except temperature kept the same.

exam.q: Suggest one improvement to the disappearing cross method and explain why it improves the results.
model: Use a light sensor / data logger (or same person, same lighting)
Removes the subjective judgement of when the cross disappears / more accurate end point
exam.tip: Improvement plus reason.

exam.q: Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid. Include how you would process the results.
model: Draw a cross on paper and place a conical flask on top
Measure a fixed volume of sodium thiosulfate into the flask and heat to a set temperature in a water bath; measure temperature with a thermometer
Add a fixed volume of hydrochloric acid and start the stop clock
Stop the clock when the cross can no longer be seen from above
Repeat at several different temperatures (and repeat each to get a mean), keeping volumes and concentrations the same
Calculate rate as 1/time and plot against temperature; ventilate the room because sulfur dioxide is produced
exam.tip: Level-marked: cover method in order, control variables, and how results become a rate.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain how to find the rate of reaction at 20 s from a graph of volume of gas against time.
model: Draw a tangent to the curve at 20 s
Calculate the gradient of the tangent
Gradient = change in volume ÷ change in time (units cm3/s)
exam.tip: Draw a long tangent to make reading the gradient more accurate.

worked.q: A student reacted 5.0 g of small marble chips with 50 cm3 of hydrochloric acid. Volumes of CO2: 0 s, 0 cm3; 20 s, 36 cm3; 40 s, 58 cm3; 60 s, 70 cm3; 80 s, 75 cm3; 100 s, 75 cm3. Calculate the mean rate over the first 40 s and over the whole reaction.
steps: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time taken.
First 40 s: 58 cm3 ÷ 40 s = 1.45 cm3/s
The reaction finished at 80 s (volume stopped changing at 75 cm3).
Whole reaction: 75 cm3 ÷ 80 s = 0.94 cm3/s (to 2 s.f.)
The rate is higher at the start because the concentration of acid is highest then; it slows as reactants are used up.
worked.ans: 1.45 cm3/s over the first 40 s; about 0.94 cm3/s over the whole reaction (80 s).

worked.q: Disappearing cross results: 20 °C, 120 s; 30 °C, 60 s; 40 °C, 30 s; 50 °C, 15 s. Calculate 1/time for each and describe the pattern.
steps: Rate is proportional to 1/time.
Each 10 °C rise halves the time, so the rate doubles.
worked.ans: Rates 0.0083, 0.017, 0.033, 0.067 s-1; as temperature increases the rate increases, roughly doubling for each 10 °C rise.

worked.q: Model answer: A student uses large chips, then powder, of the same mass with the same acid. Describe and explain how the two curves on a volume-time graph would differ.
steps: The powder curve has a steeper initial gradient than the large chips curve.
This shows the rate is faster with powder.
Powder has a larger surface area for the same mass, so more acid particles can collide with the marble at once (more frequent collisions).
The powder curve levels off sooner, because the reaction finishes sooner.
Both curves level off at the same final volume, because the same amounts of reactants form the same amount of carbon dioxide.
worked.ans: Powder: steeper curve that levels off sooner, at the same final volume as the large chips, because a larger surface area increases the rate but not the amount of product.

chem_edx.7.1.summary: The **rate of a reaction** tells you how quickly reactants are used up or products are made. You can never watch particles directly, so in the lab you measure something that changes as the reaction goes: the **volume of gas** given off (gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder), the **loss in mass** as gas escapes (top-pan balance), or the **time taken for a precipitate or colour** to appear (disappearing cross). Edexcel expects you to choose a suitable method for a given reaction, explain why it works, and calculate a **mean rate** from your results.

core.p: Rate is a measure of how fast a reaction happens. It is found by measuring how much reactant is used up, or how much product is formed, in a certain time. A fast reaction (like an explosion) is over in a fraction of a second; a slow one (like rusting) may take weeks.
bullets: **Mean rate of reaction = amount of reactant used / time taken**
or **mean rate of reaction = amount of product formed / time taken**
The 'amount' can be a **volume of gas** (cm3), a **mass** (g) or an amount in **moles** (mol).
Units follow from the quantities: cm3/s, g/s, mol/s (or per minute if time is in minutes).
Rate is usually **fastest at the start**, when there are most reactant particles, and slows down as reactants are used up.
In a practical you pick a property that **changes in a measurable way** as the reaction proceeds and record it against time.

callouts.p: The change in the amount of a reactant or product per unit time.
Either measure how fast a **product appears** (gas volume, precipitate) or how fast a **reactant disappears** (mass lost, colour fading).

core.h: Choosing a method: what can you measure?
core.p: The method you choose depends on what the reaction makes. Ask yourself: is a gas produced? Is a solid (precipitate) formed? Does the colour change? Exam questions often give you an equation and ask you to suggest a method, so look at the state symbols.
bullets: Product contains **(g)** -> measure **volume of gas** with a gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder, or measure **mass lost** on a balance.
Product contains a solid **(s)** forming in a clear solution -> **disappearing cross** (time for the cross to be hidden by the precipitate).
A coloured reactant or product -> time how long a **colour change** takes (or use a colorimeter).
A reaction that uses up acid -> could follow the **pH change** with a pH meter.
Choose the method that gives the **most precise** readings for that reaction: a gas syringe usually beats counting bubbles.

core.h: Method 1: measuring gas volume with a gas syringe
core.p: The reaction takes place in a conical flask sealed with a bung. A delivery tube leads the gas into a **gas syringe**, and the plunger is pushed out as gas collects. You read the volume on the syringe scale at regular time intervals, for example every 10 seconds, using a stopwatch.
bullets: Add the solid to the acid, **immediately** replace the bung and start the stopwatch at the same time.
Read the volume of gas every 10 s (or 30 s) until no more gas is given off (the volume stops changing).
Gas syringes are usually graduated to the nearest **1 cm3**, so they give precise readings.
Make sure the bung fits tightly; a **leak** means less gas is recorded than is made.
Gas syringes typically hold about 100 cm3, so use amounts that will not overfill it.
Plot volume of gas against time; the steeper the line, the faster the rate.

callouts.p: Some gas escapes in the moment between adding the solid and putting the bung back. This makes the measured volume slightly too low. It is a **systematic** error if it happens the same way every time.

core.h: Method 2: collecting gas in an upturned measuring cylinder
core.p: If you do not have a gas syringe, gas can be collected **over water**. A measuring cylinder (or burette) is filled with water and turned upside down in a trough of water. The delivery tube goes under its open end, and gas bubbles up and pushes the water out. The volume of gas is read from the scale.
bullets: Fill the measuring cylinder completely with water before inverting it, so no air is trapped at the start.
Read the gas volume at the **bottom of the gas space**, which is the top of the water level (the cylinder is upside down, so the scale reads downwards).
Only suitable for gases that are **not very soluble** in water, such as hydrogen and oxygen. Carbon dioxide dissolves slightly, so some is lost.
Less precise than a gas syringe because the scale may be harder to read and bubbles can miss the cylinder.
Counting bubbles is a cruder version of this; it is **not reliable** because bubbles vary in size.

callouts.p: Do not choose collection over water for a gas that dissolves well in water (such as ammonia or a lot of carbon dioxide): the measured volume would be too low.

core.h: Method 3: measuring loss of mass on a balance
core.p: When a reaction gives off a gas into the air, the mass of the flask and its contents **decreases** as the gas escapes. The flask is placed on a **top-pan balance** and the mass is recorded at regular time intervals. The faster the mass falls, the faster the reaction.
bullets: Classic example: **calcium carbonate (marble chips) + hydrochloric acid**: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
A **cotton wool plug** in the neck of the flask lets the gas out but stops acid spray (droplets) escaping, which would also lower the mass and give a false result.
Mass lost = starting mass - mass at time t. This equals the mass of gas given off.
Works best with a **dense gas** such as carbon dioxide, because the mass change is large enough to measure.
Poor for **hydrogen**: it has a very small mass, so the change may be too small for the balance to detect.

Advantage: the balance gives precise readings (often to 0.01 g) and can be logged by a computer. Disadvantage: the gas is released into the room, so it is not suitable for toxic gases without a fume cupboard.

callouts.p: Mass is conserved in a reaction, but here the system is **open**: the gas product leaves the flask, so the balance reading falls.

core.p: Some reactions between two clear solutions produce an insoluble solid called a **precipitate**, which makes the mixture go cloudy. A cross is drawn on paper and the flask is placed on top. You look down through the solution and time how long it takes for the cross to **disappear** from view.
bullets: Classic example: **sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid**: Na2S2O3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) + SO2(g) + S(s)
The yellow **sulfur** precipitate builds up until the cross can no longer be seen.
Start the stopwatch the moment the acid is added and stop it when the cross is no longer visible.
The **shorter the time**, the **faster** the rate. A simple measure of rate is **1 / time** (units s^-1).
Use the **same cross**, the same flask, the same volume of solution and the **same person** watching each time, because judging when the cross 'disappears' is subjective.
Sulfur dioxide is produced, so work in a well-ventilated room; people with asthma should take care.

callouts.p: This method gives only the **total time** for one fixed amount of precipitate to form, not a set of readings over time, so you cannot plot a curve for one run. It is used to **compare** rates under different conditions.

core.h: Other methods: colour change and pH
core.p: Any property that changes steadily during a reaction can be used to follow its rate. These are less common in Edexcel questions but are worth knowing so you can suggest a method for an unfamiliar reaction.
bullets: **Colour change**: if a reactant or product is coloured, time how long it takes for the colour to appear or disappear. A **colorimeter** measures colour intensity more objectively than the eye.
**pH change**: if an acid is used up (or an alkali formed), a **pH meter or pH probe** with a data logger can track the pH over time.
**Temperature change** is NOT a measure of rate; it tells you about energy changes (exothermic or endothermic), not how fast the reaction goes.
Data loggers and sensors record many readings automatically, reducing human reaction-time error.

callouts.p: Name the property that changes, say what apparatus measures it, and state that readings are taken at regular time intervals with a stopwatch. That structure earns most method marks.

core.p: Edexcel asks you to calculate the **mean rate** of reaction from data. Divide the change in amount (of product formed or reactant used) by the time taken. Always include units.
bullets: Example: 60 cm3 of hydrogen is collected in 30 s. Mean rate = 60 / 30 = **2.0 cm3/s**.
Example: mass falls from 120.50 g to 119.30 g in 2 minutes. Mass lost = 1.20 g. Mean rate = 1.20 / 2 = **0.60 g/min** (or 1.20 / 120 = 0.010 g/s).
Example: the cross disappears after 40 s. Rate = 1 / 40 = **0.025 s^-1**.
Convert units carefully: 1 minute = 60 s; 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3.
The mean rate over the whole reaction hides the fact that it was faster at the start and slower at the end.
Higher tier: the rate at one particular instant is found from the **gradient of a tangent** to the curve (covered in graph interpretation).

callouts.p: mean rate = quantity of product formed / time taken  or  mean rate = quantity of reactant used / time taken

core.h: Making the investigation a fair test
core.p: Rate methods are used to compare how changing one condition affects the speed of reaction. To be valid, only the **independent variable** is changed and everything else is kept the same.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the factor you change (for example acid concentration, temperature or size of marble chips).
**Dependent variable**: what you measure (volume of gas, mass lost, time for cross to disappear).
**Control variables**: volume of acid, mass of solid, size of solid pieces, temperature, type of flask, same balance or syringe.
Repeat each experiment and calculate a **mean**, ignoring anomalous results, to improve reliability (repeatability).
Start the stopwatch at exactly the same point each time (when the reactants are mixed).

head: Variable type
Example (marble chips + acid)
rows: Volume of CO2 collected every 10 s

core.h: Comparing the methods: precision and errors
core.p: Each method has strengths and weaknesses. Exam questions often ask you to evaluate a method or suggest an improvement. Think about how precise the instrument is and what could make the reading wrong.
bullets: **Gas syringe**: precise (to 1 cm3) and collects all gas, but can stick or overfill; gas can escape before the bung is fitted.
**Measuring cylinder over water**: cheap and easy, but gas may dissolve and the scale is harder to read.
**Mass loss**: very precise balance and easy to log, but needs a dense gas and the gas escapes into the room.
**Disappearing cross**: simple and cheap, but the end point is **subjective** (depends on the observer's eyesight) and gives one reading per run.
**Human reaction time** in starting and stopping the stopwatch adds random error to all timed methods.
Improvement ideas: use a data logger, a light sensor instead of the eye, a smaller scale division, or repeat and take a mean.

callouts.p: Never just say a method is 'more accurate'. Say **why**: for example 'a gas syringe has a finer scale so readings are more precise'.

core.p: A good method answer includes sensible safety precautions linked to the actual hazards.
bullets: Wear **eye protection** because acids are irritants or corrosive.
Sulfur dioxide from the thiosulfate reaction is toxic and can trigger asthma: ventilate the room and do not breathe it in.
Hydrogen is flammable: keep flames away.
When heating solutions to change temperature, use a water bath rather than a naked flame and do not exceed about 60 degrees C.
Do not let a gas syringe be pushed out of its barrel; choose amounts that produce less gas than its capacity.

analogy.p: Imagine measuring how fast a cinema empties after a film. You could count people coming out of the door each minute (like collecting the gas product), or weigh the cinema and watch its mass fall as people leave (like the mass loss method), or simply time how long until the last seat is empty (like the disappearing cross, which gives one total time). Each gives you the speed of emptying in a different way. Where it breaks down: people leave one at a time and you can see them, whereas reacting particles are far too small to count, so chemists must rely on a bulk property like gas volume or mass that changes as billions of particles react.

Quantity of reactant used or product formed divided by the time taken.
A graduated syringe whose plunger moves out as gas enters, used to measure gas volume precisely.
A tube that carries gas from the reaction vessel to the collecting apparatus.
Collecting gas in an inverted, water-filled measuring cylinder; the gas pushes the water out.
An electronic balance used to measure the mass of the flask and contents as gas escapes.
A plug in the flask neck that lets gas escape but stops acid spray leaving, so only gas loss changes the mass.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react.
A method that times how long a precipitate takes to hide a cross drawn under the flask.
The variable you deliberately change in an investigation.
The variable you measure, which changes as a result of the independent variable.
A variable kept the same so that the test is fair.
How close repeated measurements are to each other; a finer scale gives more precise readings.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, such as gas lost each time before the bung is fitted.
Unpredictable variation in readings, such as differences in human reaction time with a stopwatch.
A device that records readings from a sensor automatically at set time intervals.

mistakes.w: Rate is how long a reaction takes.
mistakes.r: Rate is the amount of reactant used or product formed **per unit time**; a longer time means a slower rate.

mistakes.w: In the disappearing cross, a longer time means a faster reaction.
mistakes.r: A **shorter** time for the cross to disappear means a **faster** rate (rate is proportional to 1/time).

mistakes.w: Measure the temperature to find the rate.
mistakes.r: Measure **volume of gas**, **mass lost** or **time for precipitate**; temperature change shows energy transfer, not rate.

mistakes.w: The cotton wool stops gas escaping.
mistakes.r: The cotton wool **lets gas escape** but **stops acid spray** escaping, so only the gas causes the mass loss.

mistakes.w: Use mass loss to follow the reaction of magnesium with acid.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen has a very low mass, so the mass change is too small to measure accurately; **collect the gas in a gas syringe** instead.

mistakes.w: Mean rate = time / volume.
mistakes.r: Mean rate = **volume (or mass) / time**, with units such as cm3/s or g/s.

mistakes.w: The mass goes down because mass is destroyed.
mistakes.r: Mass is conserved; the mass reading falls because **gas escapes** from the open flask.

mistakes.w: Count the bubbles to measure the rate accurately.
mistakes.r: Bubbles vary in size so counting is unreliable; **measure the gas volume** with a gas syringe.

mistakes.w: Repeating makes results more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeating and finding a mean improves **repeatability** and lets you spot anomalies; it reduces the effect of random errors.

exam.q: State the meaning of the term rate of reaction.
model: The amount of reactant used up or product formed per unit time.
exam.tip: Include the idea of time: 'per second' or 'per unit time'.

exam.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas. Name a piece of apparatus that could be used to measure the volume of hydrogen produced.
model: Gas syringe (or upturned measuring cylinder / burette filled with water).
exam.tip: A gas syringe is the expected answer; 'measuring cylinder' alone is not enough unless you say it is inverted over water.

exam.q: In an experiment, 48 cm3 of carbon dioxide was collected in 2 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of reaction in cm3/s.
model: Converts time: 2 minutes = 120 s.
Mean rate = 48 / 120 = 0.40 cm3/s.
exam.tip: Check the units asked for before dividing.

exam.q: Marble chips react with hydrochloric acid in a conical flask on a balance. Explain why the mass of the flask and contents decreases during the reaction.
model: Carbon dioxide gas is produced.
The gas escapes from the flask into the air.
exam.tip: Mention the gas by name and that it leaves the flask.

exam.q: Explain why a cotton wool plug is placed in the neck of the flask in the mass loss method.
model: Allows the gas (carbon dioxide) to escape.
Stops acid spray/droplets escaping, which would cause extra mass loss.
exam.tip: Two jobs: lets gas out, keeps liquid in.

exam.q: Sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form a precipitate of sulfur. Describe how the rate of this reaction can be measured.
model: Draw a cross on paper and place the flask on top.
Add the acid and start the stopwatch at the same time.
Time how long it takes for the cross to disappear when viewed from above.
exam.tip: Say where you look from (above) and when timing starts and stops.

exam.q: A student uses the disappearing cross method. Suggest one reason why their results may not be repeatable and how this could be improved.
model: Judging when the cross disappears is subjective / depends on the observer.
Use the same person each time or use a light sensor/data logger.
exam.tip: Pair each weakness with a matching improvement.

exam.q: Explain why collecting gas over water is not a good method for measuring the volume of carbon dioxide produced.
model: Carbon dioxide is (slightly) soluble in water.
So some gas dissolves and the measured volume is too low.
exam.tip: Link the property (solubility) to the effect on the result.

exam.q: Suggest why the mass loss method is not suitable for measuring the rate of the reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid.
model: The gas produced is hydrogen, which has a very low density/mass.
So the change in mass would be too small to measure accurately.
exam.tip: Identify the gas first, then explain the problem.

exam.q: Devise a method to investigate how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of its reaction with calcium carbonate. Your answer should include how you would make it a fair test.
model: Measure a fixed volume of acid (e.g. 50 cm3) with a measuring cylinder into a conical flask.
Add a fixed mass of marble chips of the same size and immediately fit a bung connected to a gas syringe.
Start the stopwatch as the chips are added.
Record the volume of gas every 10 s (or measure mass loss on a balance every 10 s).
Repeat with different concentrations of acid, keeping temperature, mass and size of chips and volume of acid the same.
Repeat each concentration and calculate a mean; plot volume against time / compare mean rates.
exam.tip: Six-mark method questions need apparatus, measurements, timing, the variable changed, the controls and how results are processed.

worked.q: A student reacts magnesium ribbon with excess hydrochloric acid and collects hydrogen in a gas syringe. Readings: 0 s 0 cm3; 10 s 18 cm3; 20 s 32 cm3; 30 s 42 cm3; 40 s 48 cm3; 50 s 50 cm3; 60 s 50 cm3. Calculate the mean rate over the first 50 s and over the first 10 s, and explain the difference.
steps: Mean rate over 50 s = volume / time = 50 / 50 = 1.0 cm3/s.
Mean rate over first 10 s = 18 / 10 = 1.8 cm3/s.
The rate is faster at the start because there are more reactant particles (more magnesium and acid) so more frequent collisions.
As magnesium is used up, collisions become less frequent and the rate falls until the reaction stops at 50 cm3.
worked.ans: 1.0 cm3/s over 50 s; 1.8 cm3/s over the first 10 s. The reaction is fastest at the start and slows as reactants are used up.

worked.q: In a mass loss experiment, the flask and contents had a mass of 152.40 g at the start and 151.25 g after 5 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of reaction in g/min and in g/s.
steps: Mass lost = 152.40 - 151.25 = 1.15 g (this is the mass of carbon dioxide given off).
Mean rate in g/min = 1.15 / 5 = 0.23 g/min.
Time in seconds = 5 x 60 = 300 s.
worked.ans: 0.23 g/min, which is 0.00383 g/s.

worked.q: In the disappearing cross experiment, the cross disappeared after 25 s at 40 degrees C and after 80 s at 20 degrees C. Calculate 1/time for each and state which is faster.
steps: At 40 degrees C: rate = 1 / 25 = 0.040 s^-1.
At 20 degrees C: rate = 1 / 80 = 0.0125 s^-1.
The larger value of 1/time means the faster rate.
worked.ans: 0.040 s^-1 at 40 degrees C and 0.0125 s^-1 at 20 degrees C; the reaction at 40 degrees C is faster (about 3.2 times faster).

chem_edx.7.2.summary: **Collision theory** says that particles can only react when they **collide** with each other, and the collision must have at least a minimum amount of energy, the **activation energy**. Most collisions do not have enough energy, so they do not lead to a reaction. The rate of a reaction depends on the **frequency of successful collisions**: increasing **concentration**, **pressure** (for gases) or **surface area to volume ratio** makes collisions more frequent, while increasing **temperature** makes particles collide more often AND with more energy, so a greater proportion of collisions succeed.

core.p: For a chemical reaction to take place, the reactant particles (atoms, ions or molecules) must physically **collide** with each other. But simply bumping into each other is not enough. The collision must be **energetic enough** to break bonds in the reactants so that new bonds can form in the products.
bullets: Particles must **collide** before they can react.
The collision must have energy **equal to or greater than the activation energy**.
A collision with enough energy that leads to a reaction is called a **successful collision**.
Most collisions are **unsuccessful**: the particles simply bounce apart unchanged.
The **rate** of reaction depends on how many successful collisions happen **per second** (the frequency of successful collisions).
Anything that increases the frequency of collisions, or the energy of collisions, increases the rate.

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide in order to react.

callouts.t: Two ways to speed up a reaction
callouts.p: Make collisions **more frequent** (more collisions per second) or make collisions **more energetic** (a greater proportion have at least the activation energy).

core.p: Grade 9 answers clearly separate two ideas. **Frequency** means how often particles collide (number of collisions per second). **Energy** means how hard they collide, which decides whether a collision is successful. Concentration, pressure and surface area only change the frequency. Temperature changes both.
bullets: Always say **'more frequent collisions'** or **'more collisions per second'**, not just 'more collisions'. The mark scheme rewards the idea of time.
Increasing frequency means more successful collisions per second even if the **proportion** that succeed stays the same.
Increasing energy means a **greater proportion** (fraction) of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
Catalysts work differently: they provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy (covered in 7.6-7.7).

callouts.p: Higher concentration does NOT give particles more energy. Only temperature (of these four factors) changes the energy of collisions.

core.p: The **concentration** of a solution tells you how many particles of solute are dissolved in a given volume. A more concentrated solution has **more reactant particles in the same volume**, so the particles are closer together.
bullets: Higher concentration -> more particles in the same volume.
So particles collide **more frequently** (more collisions per second).
So there are **more successful collisions per second**.
So the **rate of reaction increases**.
Example: magnesium reacts faster with 2.0 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid than with 0.5 mol/dm3 acid.

If the solid is in excess and acid is limiting, doubling acid concentration (same volume) also doubles the total amount of product; with the acid in excess, the final amount of product is unchanged and only the rate changes.

callouts.p: Write the chain every time: **more particles in the same volume -> more frequent collisions -> more successful collisions per second -> faster rate**.

core.p: For reactions between **gases**, increasing the **pressure** has the same effect as increasing concentration. The same number of gas particles are squashed into a **smaller volume**, so they are closer together.
bullets: Higher pressure -> same number of particles in a smaller volume (more particles per unit volume).
So particles collide **more frequently**.
So there are **more successful collisions per second** and the rate increases.
Pressure only affects reactions where at least one **reactant is a gas**. It has almost no effect on reactions between solids and liquids.
Industrial example: the Haber process (making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen) uses high pressure partly to increase the rate.

callouts.p: Increasing pressure does not make particles move faster or collide harder; it just packs them closer together.

core.h: Effect of surface area to volume ratio
core.p: When a **solid** reacts with a liquid or gas, only the particles on the **surface** of the solid can be hit by the other reactant. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces (or a powder) exposes more surface for the same mass, so it has a **larger surface area to volume ratio**.
bullets: Smaller pieces / powder -> **larger surface area to volume ratio**.
More solid particles are **exposed** to the other reactant.
So collisions happen **more frequently** (more collisions per second).
So more successful collisions per second and a **faster rate**.
Example: marble powder fizzes much faster with acid than large marble chips of the same mass.
Real-world hazards: fine powders such as flour, custard powder or coal dust can react explosively with air because of their huge surface area.

callouts.p: The surface area of a solid divided by its volume; smaller pieces have a larger ratio.
Edexcel wording is **surface area to volume ratio**. Do not write 'bigger surface area particles' or say the particles themselves get smaller.

core.p: Temperature has the **biggest effect** of all these factors because it changes both the frequency and the energy of collisions. When you heat a reaction mixture, particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
bullets: Higher temperature -> particles have **more kinetic energy** and **move faster**.
Faster particles collide **more frequently** (more collisions per second).
Collisions are also **more energetic**: a **greater proportion** of collisions have energy **equal to or greater than the activation energy**.
Both effects give **more successful collisions per second**, so the rate increases.
The energy effect is the more important one: a small rise in temperature greatly increases the fraction of particles with enough energy to react.
A rough rule of thumb is that a 10 degrees C rise roughly doubles the rate of many reactions, but you do not need to learn this for Edexcel.

callouts.p: Full marks need BOTH ideas: particles collide **more frequently** AND **more collisions have at least the activation energy**.

core.p: At any temperature, particles in a substance have a **range of energies**: some are slow, most are medium, a few are very fast. Only collisions involving particles with enough energy (at least the activation energy) can break the bonds needed to react.
bullets: In a typical reaction at room temperature only a tiny fraction of collisions are successful.
Particles also need to meet **the right way round** in some reactions, but Edexcel GCSE focuses on frequency and energy.
Raising the temperature shifts the spread of energies upwards, so many more particles exceed the activation energy.
Lowering the activation energy (with a catalyst) also means more particles have enough energy, without heating.

callouts.p: A collision between reactant particles that has at least the activation energy and so results in a reaction.

core.h: Why the rate slows down as a reaction proceeds
core.p: Collision theory also explains why reactions slow down and stop. As the reaction goes on, reactant particles are used up, so the concentration of reactants falls.
bullets: Fewer reactant particles remain in the same volume.
So collisions become **less frequent** and there are fewer successful collisions per second.
The rate decreases, so the gradient of a volume-time graph gets less steep.
The reaction **stops** when one reactant (the **limiting reactant**) is completely used up.

core.p: Collision theory is what you use to **explain** the results of rate experiments, such as the core practical on changing acid concentration or the disappearing cross with changing temperature.
bullets: Marble chips + hydrochloric acid: higher acid concentration -> more gas per second -> explain with more frequent collisions.
Sodium thiosulfate + acid: higher temperature -> cross disappears faster -> explain with frequency AND energy.
Powdered versus lumps of calcium carbonate: powder gives faster rate -> explain with surface area to volume ratio.
When you **describe** a result, say what happens (rate increases). When you **explain**, use particles and collisions.

callouts.p: Describe = what the data shows. Explain = why, using particles, frequency of collisions and activation energy.

core.p: Changing conditions changes **how fast** the product forms, but it does not necessarily change **how much** product is made in the end. That is fixed by the amount of limiting reactant.
bullets: Smaller pieces of the same mass of marble give the **same final volume** of CO2, just more quickly.
Higher temperature with the same amounts of reactants gives the **same final amount** of product.
Using more of the limiting reactant (for example more moles of acid when acid is limiting) gives **more** product.
On a graph, faster rate = steeper start; same amount of product = curve levels off at the same height.

callouts.p: Do not say crushing the marble 'makes more gas'. It makes the same amount of gas, faster.

core.h: Controlling rates in everyday life and industry
core.p: Chemists and engineers use collision theory to make useful reactions faster and unwanted reactions slower.
bullets: Food is kept in a **fridge** because lower temperature slows the reactions that cause it to spoil.
Cooking food at higher temperature (or cutting it into small pieces) makes it cook faster.
Industrial processes use higher temperatures, higher pressures (gases) and catalysts to make products quickly and economically.
Flour mills and coal mines must control dust because powders with a large surface area to volume ratio can explode.

analogy.p: Think of a dodgem arena. Putting more cars in the same arena (higher concentration or pressure) means they bump into each other more often. Opening up more entrances to a crowded room (larger surface area) lets more people meet those inside per minute. Turning up the speed of the cars (higher temperature) means they bump more often AND hit hard enough to really jolt the riders, like collisions with enough energy to react. Where it breaks down: dodgems never 'react' or change into new cars, and in a real reaction only collisions above a fixed energy threshold (the activation energy) succeed, while the rest are completely unproductive.

terms.d: The idea that particles must collide with at least the activation energy in order to react.
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react.
A collision with at least the activation energy that leads to a reaction.
The number of collisions between particles per second.
How much energy particles have when they collide; decides whether a collision is successful.
How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed per unit time.
The amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, e.g. in mol/dm3 or g/dm3.
Caused by gas particles hitting the walls of a container; higher pressure means more gas particles per unit volume.
Surface area divided by volume; larger for smaller pieces or powders.
Energy a particle has because it is moving; increases with temperature.
The reactant that is completely used up and so determines when the reaction stops and how much product forms.
The reactant that is left over when the reaction stops.
The fraction of all collisions that have at least the activation energy; increased by raising temperature.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, by providing a pathway with lower activation energy.

mistakes.w: Higher temperature means more collisions.
mistakes.r: Higher temperature means **more frequent** collisions AND a **greater proportion** of collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy.

mistakes.w: Higher concentration gives particles more energy.
mistakes.r: Higher concentration gives **more particles in the same volume**, so **more frequent collisions**; energy is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Smaller pieces have a smaller surface area so react faster.
mistakes.r: Smaller pieces have a **larger surface area to volume ratio**, so more particles are exposed and collisions are more frequent.

mistakes.w: The particles collide harder at higher pressure.
mistakes.r: At higher pressure particles are **closer together (more per unit volume)**, so they collide **more frequently**; collision energy is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Particles react every time they collide.
mistakes.r: Only collisions with energy **equal to or greater than the activation energy** are successful.

mistakes.w: Crushing marble chips produces more carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: It produces the **same total volume** of CO2, but **faster**.

mistakes.w: The particles move faster at higher concentration.
mistakes.r: Speed depends on temperature; concentration only changes **how many particles** are in a given volume.

mistakes.w: Activation energy is the energy given out by the reaction.
mistakes.r: Activation energy is the **minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful**.

mistakes.w: Increasing pressure speeds up any reaction.
mistakes.r: Pressure only affects the rate of reactions involving **gases**.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term activation energy.
model: The minimum energy needed (by colliding particles) for a reaction to occur.
exam.tip: The key word is 'minimum'.

exam.q: State two things that must happen for particles to react.
model: Particles must collide.
With energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
exam.tip: Collision AND enough energy.

exam.q: Explain why increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increases the rate of its reaction with magnesium.
model: More (acid) particles in the same volume.
So more frequent collisions / more collisions per second.
exam.tip: Avoid saying 'more collisions' without 'per second' or 'frequent'.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, why powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with acid than the same mass of large lumps.
model: Powder has a larger surface area to volume ratio.
More particles exposed to acid particles.
So more frequent collisions (more successful collisions per second).
exam.tip: Use the exact phrase 'surface area to volume ratio'.

exam.q: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid.
model: Particles have more (kinetic) energy / move faster.
So collide more frequently.
A greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy (more successful collisions).
exam.tip: Temperature always needs both the frequency and the energy point.

exam.q: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia. Explain why increasing the pressure increases the rate of this reaction.
model: Gas particles are closer together / more particles per unit volume.
So collisions are more frequent.
exam.tip: Pressure works just like concentration for gases.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of reaction between marble chips and acid decreases as the reaction proceeds.
model: Reactants are used up / concentration of acid decreases.
So collisions become less frequent.
exam.tip: Link the falling concentration to frequency of collisions.

exam.q: A student says that increasing the temperature of a reaction increases the rate only because the particles collide more often. Evaluate this statement.
model: Partly correct: particles do collide more frequently.
But the main reason is that more collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (a greater proportion are successful).
exam.tip: Evaluate means say what is right and what is missing.

exam.q: Explain why food lasts longer in a fridge than on a kitchen worktop.
model: Lower temperature so particles have less energy / move more slowly.
Fewer (frequent) collisions and fewer have activation energy, so reactions that spoil food are slower.
exam.tip: Apply the temperature argument in reverse.

exam.q: Explain how changes in concentration, surface area to volume ratio and temperature affect the rate of the reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid. Refer to collision theory in your answer.
model: Reactions occur when particles collide with at least the activation energy.
Higher acid concentration: more particles in the same volume, more frequent collisions, faster rate.
Smaller pieces/powder: larger surface area to volume ratio, more particles exposed, more frequent collisions, faster rate.
Higher temperature: particles move faster, more frequent collisions.
Higher temperature: greater proportion of collisions have energy at least equal to activation energy.
In each case more successful collisions per second so rate increases.
exam.tip: Structure: one short paragraph per factor, each with cause -> frequency/energy -> rate.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why 1.0 g of magnesium powder reacts faster with 50 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid than 1.0 g of magnesium ribbon, but produces the same total volume of hydrogen (acid in excess).
steps: Powder has a much larger surface area to volume ratio than ribbon.
More magnesium atoms are exposed to the acid particles at any moment.
So collisions between acid particles and magnesium are more frequent, giving more successful collisions per second and a faster rate.
The total amount of magnesium (the limiting reactant) is the same, 1.0 g, so the same amount of hydrogen is made overall.
worked.ans: Powder reacts faster because of more frequent collisions from its larger surface area to volume ratio; the volume of hydrogen is the same because the mass of magnesium (limiting reactant) is the same.

worked.q: Applied example: the time for the cross to disappear in the sodium thiosulfate reaction was 120 s at 20 degrees C and 30 s at 50 degrees C. Use collision theory to explain the difference.
steps: Describe: at 50 degrees C the cross disappears 4 times faster, so the rate is higher.
At higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy and move faster.
They collide more frequently.
A greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
So there are many more successful collisions per second and sulfur forms faster.
worked.ans: The higher temperature increases both the frequency of collisions and the proportion of collisions with at least the activation energy, so the rate is about 4 times faster (1/30 = 0.033 s^-1 compared with 1/120 = 0.0083 s^-1).

chem_edx.7.3.summary: Graphs of **mass, volume or concentration against time** show how a reaction progresses. The **gradient (slope)** of the line at any point tells you the **rate**: a steep line means a fast reaction, a shallow line means a slow one, and a **horizontal line** means the reaction has stopped because a reactant has been used up. You need to read values off these graphs, calculate **mean rates**, compare curves for different conditions and, for Higher tier, find the rate at a particular time from the **gradient of a tangent**.

core.p: In a rate experiment you record a quantity at regular time intervals and plot it against time. **Time always goes on the x-axis** (it is the independent variable). The quantity measured goes on the y-axis. The shape of the curve tells the story of the reaction from start to finish.
bullets: **Volume of gas produced** against time: the curve rises, then levels off.
**Mass of product formed** against time: the curve rises, then levels off.
**Mass of flask and contents** (gas escaping) against time: the curve falls, then levels off.
**Concentration of a reactant** against time: the curve falls towards zero (or a constant value) and levels off.
**Concentration of a product** against time: the curve rises and levels off.
Every curve is **steepest at the start** and gets **less steep** as time goes on.

head: Quantity plotted
Shape of curve
Reason
rows: Product builds up until reaction stops

callouts.p: The **gradient (steepness)** of the graph at any point is the **rate of reaction** at that moment.

fig.cap: Volume of gas against time: the curve is steepest at the start (fastest rate), becomes less steep as reactants are used up, and is horizontal once the reaction has stopped.

core.h: Reading the shape of the curve
core.p: Explain the shape in three stages, using collision theory. This is a common 3 or 4 mark question.
bullets: **Start (steepest)**: the concentration of reactants is highest, so collisions are most frequent and the rate is fastest.
**Middle (getting less steep)**: reactants are being used up, so there are fewer reactant particles and collisions become less frequent; the rate decreases.
**End (horizontal)**: one reactant (the **limiting reactant**) has been completely used up, so the reaction has **stopped** and no more product forms.
The **height** at which the curve levels off shows the **total amount of product** formed.
The time at which the curve first becomes flat is the **time the reaction finished**.

callouts.p: A horizontal line means the rate is **zero**: the reaction has finished. It does not mean the reaction is 'going slowly'.

core.p: Many marks come from simply reading the graph accurately. Use a ruler to draw lines from the axis to the curve and across to the other axis.
bullets: To find the volume at a given time: go **up** from the time on the x-axis to the curve, then **across** to the y-axis.
To find the time to reach a given volume: go **across** from the y-axis to the curve, then **down**.
To find when the reaction finished: find where the curve **first becomes horizontal** and read the time.
To find the total volume of gas: read the y-value of the **flat part** of the curve.
Check the scale on each axis carefully: one small square may be 2 cm3 or 5 s, not 1.
Give your answer to the precision the scale allows (often to half a small square).

callouts.p: Draw construction lines on the graph in the exam. Examiners can then credit a correct method even if your final reading is slightly out.

core.h: Calculating mean rate from a graph
core.p: The **mean rate** over a period is the change in the quantity divided by the time taken. It is the gradient of a straight line joining two points on the curve.
bullets: **Mean rate = change in quantity / time taken**
Mean rate over the whole reaction = total product formed / time taken for reaction to finish.
Mean rate between two times = (value at t2 - value at t1) / (t2 - t1).
Units: cm3/s for gas volume, g/s for mass, mol/dm3/s (mol dm^-3 s^-1) for concentration.
Mean rates over **early** time intervals are larger than over later intervals because the reaction slows down.
If the quantity is falling (reactant or mass of flask), use the size of the change and ignore the minus sign.

callouts.p: mean rate of reaction = amount of product formed / time taken  or  amount of reactant used / time taken

core.h: Higher tier: rate at a particular time using a tangent
core.p: Because the curve keeps changing steepness, the rate is different at every moment. To find the rate at one particular time you draw a **tangent**: a straight line that just touches the curve at that point, with the same slope as the curve there. Its gradient is the rate at that time.
bullets: Mark the point on the curve at the time you are asked about.
Place a ruler so it **touches the curve at that point only** and has the same slope; draw a long straight line.
Choose two points far apart on the tangent and draw a large right-angled triangle.
**Gradient = change in y / change in x** (read both from the axes, using their scales).
The gradient is the **rate at that time**, in units such as cm3/s.
A tangent at t = 0 gives the **initial rate**, which is the fastest rate.

callouts.p: Make the triangle as large as possible. Reading values far apart reduces the effect of small reading errors.

callouts.t: Do not use the curve itself
callouts.p: Read the triangle's corners from the **tangent line**, not from points on the curve; points on the curve give a mean rate, not the rate at an instant.

fig.cap: Higher tier: a tangent is drawn touching the curve at one time. The gradient of the tangent (change in y divided by change in x) is the rate of reaction at that moment.

core.p: Exam questions often show two or more curves on the same axes and ask which conditions each represents, or ask you to sketch a new curve. Compare the **initial gradient** (how fast) and the **final height** (how much product).
bullets: **Steeper initial gradient** = faster rate (higher temperature, higher concentration, smaller pieces, higher pressure or a catalyst).
A faster curve **levels off sooner** (reaction finishes in less time).
If the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged, both curves level off at the **same final height**.
If the amount of limiting reactant is **halved**, the curve levels off at **half the height**.
Halving the concentration of acid (same volume, acid limiting) gives a less steep start AND half the final volume.
When sketching a new curve, always start it at the **origin** (0,0).

head: Change made
Initial gradient
Final amount of product
rows: Half the mass of limiting solid
Lower concentration of acid, acid in excess

callouts.p: A catalyst, a higher temperature or smaller pieces change **how fast**, not **how much**. Draw the new curve levelling off at the same height.

fig.cap: Comparing reactions: A and B use the same amounts of reactants so end at the same volume, but A is faster (steeper start). C uses half the amount of the limiting reactant, so it produces half the volume.

core.h: Graphs of mass of flask against time
core.p: In the mass loss method the balance reading **falls** as gas escapes. The curve is the mirror image of a gas volume curve: it drops steeply at first, then more gently, then becomes flat.
bullets: Steep downward slope at the start = fast rate.
The curve becomes **horizontal** when the reaction stops; the mass then stays constant.
**Total mass lost** = starting mass - final constant mass = mass of gas given off.
Sometimes the data is plotted as **mass lost** against time instead, which gives a rising curve.
Rate from this graph = mass lost / time, in g/s.

callouts.p: Is it 'mass of flask' (falls) or 'mass lost' (rises)? Read the label before describing the trend.

fig.cap: Mass of flask and contents against time: the mass falls quickly at first as carbon dioxide escapes, then more slowly, and stays constant once the reaction has stopped.
