core.p: If you follow the concentration of a reactant (for example by titration or with a sensor), the curve falls; for a product it rises. The same rules apply: gradient = rate, flat = reaction finished.
bullets: Reactant concentration falls steeply at first and then levels off (at zero if it is the limiting reactant, or above zero if it is in excess).
Product concentration rises steeply at first and then levels off.
Rate units: mol/dm3 per second (mol dm^-3 s^-1) or g/dm3 per second.
The reactant curve and product curve are related by the equation: if 1 mol of reactant makes 1 mol of product, one falls as fast as the other rises.

core.p: You may be asked to plot results then draw a line of best fit. Accuracy here earns easy marks.
bullets: Use a scale that makes the points cover **more than half** of the grid in each direction.
Label both axes with the quantity and the **unit**, for example 'Volume of gas / cm3' and 'Time / s'.
Plot points accurately with small neat crosses.
Draw a **smooth curve of best fit** through or close to the points; do not join dot to dot.
Identify **anomalous** results that do not fit the pattern and ignore them when drawing the curve.
The curve should go through the origin for a product (no product at time zero).

callouts.p: Joining each point with straight ruler lines loses the line of best fit mark. Rate graphs are smooth curves.

core.h: Explaining differences between curves using collision theory
core.p: A full answer links the graph feature to the particle explanation. The graph shows WHAT happens; collision theory explains WHY.
bullets: Steeper curve at higher temperature: particles move faster, collide more frequently and a greater proportion of collisions have at least the activation energy.
Steeper curve at higher concentration: more particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions.
Steeper curve with powder: larger surface area to volume ratio, so more frequent collisions.
Steeper curve with a catalyst: an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
Same final height: the same amount of limiting reactant, so the same amount of product.

callouts.p: For 'compare the curves' questions write one sentence about the gradient (rate) and one about the final height (amount of product).

analogy.t: Filling a bucket from a water butt
analogy.p: Imagine filling a bucket from a water butt that is emptying. At first the butt is full, the pressure is high and water gushes out fast, so the bucket's water level rises steeply. As the butt empties, the flow slows and the level rises more gently. When the butt is empty the level stays flat. The steepness of the 'water level against time' graph is the flow rate, just as the gradient of a volume-time graph is the rate of reaction, and the final level is set by how much water was in the butt (the limiting reactant). Where it breaks down: the water flow slows because of falling pressure, whereas a reaction slows because fewer reactant particles mean less frequent collisions.

terms.d: The change in amount of reactant or product per unit time; the gradient of an amount-time graph.
The steepness of a line: change in y divided by change in x.
Total change in quantity divided by the time taken; the gradient of a straight line between two points on the curve.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
The rate at the very start of the reaction (t = 0); the fastest rate, found from a tangent at the origin.
The gradient of the tangent to the curve at that time (Higher tier).
The point where the curve becomes horizontal, showing the reaction has stopped.
The reactant used up first; it decides when the reaction stops and how much product forms.
A smooth line or curve drawn close to as many points as possible, showing the overall trend.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others.
The variable plotted on the x-axis; here, time.
The variable plotted on the y-axis; the quantity measured, such as volume of gas.
Lines drawn on a graph from the axis to the curve to read off values.
The point (0,0) where the axes meet; product curves start here.

mistakes.w: The flat part of the graph shows the reaction is slow.
mistakes.r: The flat part shows the reaction has **stopped** because a reactant (the limiting reactant) has been **used up**.

mistakes.w: The rate is the highest point on the graph.
mistakes.r: The rate is the **gradient** of the graph; the highest point is the **total amount of product**.

mistakes.w: A catalyst makes the curve finish higher.
mistakes.r: A catalyst makes the curve **steeper** but it levels off at the **same final height**.

mistakes.w: The reaction slows down because the particles get tired / lose energy.
mistakes.r: It slows down because reactants are **used up**, so there are fewer particles and **less frequent collisions**.

mistakes.w: Rate at 20 s = volume at 20 s / 20.
mistakes.r: That gives the **mean rate** over the first 20 s; the rate **at** 20 s is the gradient of the **tangent** at 20 s.

mistakes.w: Joining all the plotted points with a ruler.
mistakes.r: Draw a **smooth curve of best fit**, ignoring anomalous points.

mistakes.w: Sketched faster curve not starting at zero.
mistakes.r: Any product curve must **start at the origin** because no product exists at time zero.

mistakes.w: Using points on the curve to calculate a tangent's gradient.
mistakes.r: Read both corners of the triangle from the **tangent line** itself, using a large triangle.

exam.q: State how the rate of reaction can be found from a graph of volume of gas against time.
model: From the gradient/slope of the graph (steeper = faster).
exam.tip: Gradient is the key word.

exam.q: Explain why the graph of volume of gas against time becomes horizontal.
model: The reaction has stopped / no more gas is produced.
Because one reactant (limiting reactant) has been used up.
exam.tip: Give both what happens and why.

exam.q: A reaction produced 75 cm3 of gas in total and finished after 150 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.
model: Mean rate = 75 / 150.
exam.tip: Always include units.

exam.q: Describe how the rate of reaction changes during the reaction, as shown by a volume of gas against time curve.
model: Rate is fastest at the start (steepest).
Rate decreases (gradient falls) until it is zero when the line is flat.
exam.tip: Use the words 'steep' and 'gradient'.

exam.q: Explain, using collision theory, why the gradient of the curve decreases as the reaction proceeds.
model: Reactant particles are used up.
Concentration of reactants decreases / fewer particles in the same volume.
So collisions are less frequent, so the rate decreases.
exam.tip: Link fewer particles to less frequent collisions.

exam.q: On the same axes as curve A, sketch the curve you would expect if the experiment was repeated at a higher temperature with the same amounts of reactants.
model: Curve starts at origin and is steeper than A initially.
Levels off at the same final volume as A (and sooner).
exam.tip: Two features to show: steeper start, same final height.

exam.q: The experiment was repeated with half the mass of magnesium (magnesium is the limiting reactant), all other conditions the same. Describe how the new curve compares with the original.
model: Levels off at half the final volume.
Initial gradient is less steep / reaction slower (smaller surface area of magnesium).
exam.tip: Halving the limiting reactant halves the total product.

exam.q: Higher: Describe how you would use the graph to find the rate of reaction at 30 s.
model: Draw a tangent to the curve at 30 s.
Draw a (large) triangle on the tangent and read the change in y and change in x.
Rate = change in y / change in x (gradient of the tangent).
exam.tip: Mention 'tangent' and 'gradient'.

exam.q: Higher: A tangent drawn at 20 s passes through (0 s, 10 cm3) and (40 s, 58 cm3). Calculate the rate of reaction at 20 s.
exam.tip: Subtract in the same order on top and bottom.

exam.q: Two experiments were carried out with marble chips and excess hydrochloric acid: one with large chips and one with the same mass of small chips. Their volume-time graphs are drawn on the same axes. Describe and explain the differences between the two curves.
model: Small chips curve has a steeper initial gradient, showing a faster rate.
Small chips curve levels off sooner (reaction finishes in less time).
Both curves level off at the same final volume.
Small chips have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so more particles are exposed to acid.
So collisions are more frequent, giving more successful collisions per second.
Same mass of calcium carbonate (limiting reactant), so same amount of carbon dioxide produced.
exam.tip: Describe gradient, finish time and final height, then explain each one.

exam.q: A graph shows the mass of a flask and its contents falling from 85.40 g to 84.20 g, after which it stays constant. State the mass of carbon dioxide produced.
exam.tip: Mass lost = mass of gas given off.

worked.q: Hydrogen gas volumes: 0 s 0 cm3; 20 s 30 cm3; 40 s 48 cm3; 60 s 57 cm3; 80 s 60 cm3; 100 s 60 cm3. (a) When did the reaction stop? (b) Calculate the mean rate over the first 20 s and between 40 s and 60 s. (c) Calculate the mean rate for the whole reaction.
steps: (a) The volume first reaches its constant value of 60 cm3 at 80 s, so the reaction stopped at (or just before) 80 s.
The later rate is smaller because reactants have been used up, so collisions are less frequent.
(c) Whole reaction: 60 cm3 / 80 s = 0.75 cm3/s.
worked.ans: (a) About 80 s. (b) 1.5 cm3/s, then 0.45 cm3/s. (c) 0.75 cm3/s.

worked.q: Higher: A tangent is drawn to a volume-time curve at 50 s. Two points on the tangent are (10 s, 20 cm3) and (90 s, 68 cm3). Calculate the rate of reaction at 50 s.
steps: Change in y = 68 - 20 = 48 cm3.
Change in x = 90 - 10 = 80 s.
Gradient = 48 / 80 = 0.60.
The gradient of the tangent equals the rate at that time.
worked.ans: Rate at 50 s = 0.60 cm3/s.

worked.q: Model answer: a graph shows curve P for 1.0 mol/dm3 acid and curve Q for 0.5 mol/dm3 acid (same volume, acid is the limiting reactant, magnesium in excess). Explain why Q is less steep and finishes at half the volume of P.
steps: Q has a lower concentration, so fewer acid particles in the same volume.
So collisions are less frequent and the rate is slower: smaller initial gradient.
Q contains half the number of moles of acid (the limiting reactant).
So only half as much hydrogen can be made: the curve levels off at half the height.
worked.ans: Q is less steep because of less frequent collisions at lower concentration, and reaches half the final volume because it contains half the amount of the limiting reactant.

chem_edx.7.4.summary: A **catalyst** is a substance that speeds up the rate of a reaction without altering the products of the reaction, and is itself **unchanged chemically and in mass** at the end of the reaction. It works by providing an **alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy**, so a greater proportion of particles have enough energy to react when they collide and the frequency of successful collisions increases. Catalysts do not change the amount of product made or the overall energy change, which is why they are so valuable in industry: the same product, faster, at lower temperatures and lower cost.

core.h: What a catalyst is: the Edexcel definition
core.p: Edexcel expects a precise three-part description of a catalyst. Each part is a separate mark-scheme idea, so learn all three and say them every time. A catalyst takes part in the reaction (it is not just a spectator), but it is regenerated by the end, which is why the same tiny amount can be used again and again.
bullets: A catalyst **speeds up the rate of a reaction**.
It **does not alter the products** of the reaction: the same products form, in the same amounts.
It is **unchanged chemically** at the end of the reaction: it is the same substance it was at the start.
It is **unchanged in mass** at the end: none of it is used up, so it can be recovered and reused.
Because it is not used up, only a **small amount** of catalyst is needed.
A catalyst is **not a reactant**, so it is not written as a reactant in the equation. It is sometimes written above the arrow, e.g. 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 with MnO2 written over the arrow.
Catalysts are **specific**: a catalyst that works for one reaction usually does not work for a different reaction.

callouts.p: A substance that speeds up the rate of a reaction without altering the products of the reaction, being itself unchanged chemically and in mass at the end of the reaction.

core.h: Recap: collision theory and activation energy
core.p: To explain catalysts you need collision theory. For a reaction to happen, reactant particles must **collide**, and the collision must have **enough energy**. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide for a reaction to occur is called the **activation energy (Ea)**. Collisions with less energy than this just bounce apart without reacting. Collisions with energy equal to or greater than Ea are **successful collisions**.
bullets: Rate of reaction depends on the **frequency of successful collisions** (number of successful collisions per second).
Activation energy is an **energy barrier** that must be overcome before bonds in the reactants can start to break.
At any temperature, particles have a **range of energies**: only some have energy ≥ Ea.
The **lower** the activation energy, the **greater the proportion** of particles that have enough energy to react.
Temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area change rate by changing the frequency and/or energy of collisions (spec 7.3-7.4). A catalyst is different: it **changes the barrier itself**.

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide for a reaction to occur.

core.h: How a catalyst increases the rate (the key explanation)
core.p: This is the explanation that carries the marks. A catalyst provides a **different route** (an alternative reaction pathway) from reactants to products. This route has a **lower activation energy** than the uncatalysed route. The particles still have exactly the same range of energies as before, but now that the barrier is lower, **more of the particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy**. So a greater proportion of collisions are successful and the **frequency of successful collisions increases**, so the rate increases.
bullets: Step 1: catalyst provides an **alternative reaction pathway**.
Step 2: this pathway has a **lower activation energy**.
Step 3: so **more particles / a greater proportion of collisions** have energy ≥ the activation energy.
Step 4: so there are **more successful collisions per second** (higher frequency of successful collisions).
Step 5: so the **rate of reaction increases**.
A catalyst does **not** give the particles more energy and does **not** make them move faster: only heating does that.
A catalyst does **not** increase the total number of collisions per second; it increases the **fraction of collisions that succeed**.

callouts.p: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
Never write that a catalyst 'gives particles more energy' or 'makes particles collide more'. Both lose the mark. It lowers the activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

core.h: Reaction profile with and without a catalyst
core.p: A reaction profile shows the energy of the reactants and products and the energy barrier between them as the reaction progresses. When you add a catalyst, the **hump gets lower**, but the **reactant and product energy levels stay exactly where they were**. That means the catalyst lowers the activation energy but does **not** change the overall energy change of the reaction.
bullets: Activation energy is measured from the **reactants level up to the top of the hump** (the peak).
The catalysed curve has a **lower peak**, so a **smaller activation energy arrow**.
Reactants and products start and finish at the **same energy levels** on both curves.
So the **overall energy change (ΔH) is the same** with or without a catalyst.
A catalyst lowers activation energy for **both exothermic and endothermic** reactions, and for the forward and reverse reactions of a reversible reaction.
When drawing: label axes **energy** and **progress of reaction**, draw the activation energy arrow from reactants to peak, and draw the energy change arrow from reactants level to products level.

callouts.p: Start and end both curves at the same two levels. If your catalysed curve ends at a different product level you lose the mark, because a catalyst cannot change the energy change.

core.h: What a catalyst does NOT change
core.p: Grade 9 answers are precise about what stays the same. A catalyst only changes **how fast** equilibrium or completion is reached, not **where** the reaction ends up or how much energy is released or absorbed overall.
bullets: It does **not** change the **products** formed.
It does **not** change the **mass or amount of product** made (the final volume of gas collected is the same).
It does **not** change the **overall energy change** (the energy difference between reactants and products).
It does **not** change the **energy of the particles** or the temperature.
It is **not used up**: its mass and chemical identity are the same at the end.
In a reversible reaction it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does **not** change the position of equilibrium (useful link to topic 3 / Haber process).

core.h: Rate graphs with and without a catalyst
core.p: If you measure the volume of gas produced over time, the catalysed reaction gives a **steeper curve at the start** (higher initial rate) and **levels off sooner**, but it levels off at the **same final volume**, because the same amount of reactant is used up and the catalyst does not change the amount of product.
bullets: Steeper gradient = faster rate. Gradient of the curve at the start = initial rate.
Catalysed curve flattens **earlier**: the reaction finishes in less time.
Both curves reach the **same final height**: same amount of limiting reactant, so same amount of product.
If an exam graph shows a different final volume, something other than a catalyst has changed (e.g. the amount of reactant).
Mean rate = amount of product formed ÷ time taken (e.g. cm³/s).

callouts.p: When asked to sketch the catalysed line on an existing graph: start at the origin, draw it steeper, and level off at the same final value earlier.

core.h: Investigating catalysts: decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
core.p: The classic school experiment is the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H2O2(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g). On its own this is very slow. Adding a small amount of **manganese(IV) oxide (MnO2)**, a black powder, makes it fizz rapidly. You can compare different possible catalysts (e.g. MnO2, copper(II) oxide, lead(IV) oxide, iron(III) oxide) by measuring the **volume of oxygen** collected in a **gas syringe** (or by downward displacement of water in an upturned measuring cylinder) at regular time intervals.
bullets: Independent variable: the **type of catalyst** (or no catalyst as a control).
Dependent variable: **volume of oxygen** produced in a set time (or time to collect a fixed volume).
Control variables: **same mass** of catalyst, **same particle size / surface area** (powder), **same volume and concentration** of hydrogen peroxide, **same temperature**.
Start the stopwatch as soon as the catalyst is added and quickly reconnect the bung so gas is not lost.
To prove the substance is a catalyst: weigh it before, then **filter**, **wash**, **dry** and **reweigh** it afterwards; the mass is **unchanged**.
You can also add the recovered solid to fresh hydrogen peroxide: it still catalyses the reaction, showing it is **chemically unchanged**.
Testing the gas: oxygen **relights a glowing splint**.

callouts.p: A powdered catalyst works faster than lumps because more surface is exposed. In a fair test, use the same form (powder) and the same mass of each catalyst.

core.p: Catalysts are hugely important economically. Because they speed up reactions, industry can make products **faster** and often at **lower temperatures and pressures**, which **saves energy and money** and reduces the burning of fossil fuels (so less carbon dioxide is released). Because they are not used up, they can be used for a long time, although they can eventually be 'poisoned' by impurities.
bullets: **Haber process** (making ammonia, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3): **iron** catalyst.
**Contact process** (making sulfuric acid, 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3): **vanadium(V) oxide** catalyst.
**Catalytic converters** in cars: **platinum, palladium and rhodium** convert carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons into less harmful gases.
**Hydrogen peroxide decomposition**: manganese(IV) oxide catalyst (lab example).
Many catalysts are **transition metals or their compounds** (iron, vanadium, platinum, nickel).
Catalysts are often used as **powders, pellets or fine meshes / honeycombs** to give a **large surface area**, because reactions happen on the catalyst surface.
**Enzymes** are biological catalysts made of protein (spec point 7.8), e.g. enzymes in yeast used to make alcoholic drinks.

callouts.p: Same product, faster, at a lower temperature: lower energy costs, lower fuel use and less CO2 released. The catalyst itself is reused, so the cost of buying it is spread over a long time.

core.h: Catalysts compared with other ways of increasing rate
core.p: Examiners like you to compare how each factor works. Temperature is the only factor that increases both the frequency and the energy of collisions. Concentration, pressure and surface area increase collision frequency only. A catalyst is the only factor that **lowers the activation energy**.
bullets: Higher temperature: particles move faster, collide more often **and** more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
Higher concentration or pressure: more particles in the same volume, so **more frequent** collisions.
Larger surface area: more particles exposed, so **more frequent** collisions.
Catalyst: **lowers Ea** via an alternative pathway, so a **greater proportion** of collisions are successful.
A catalyst is often preferred over raising temperature in industry because heating costs energy and money, and for exothermic equilibrium reactions a high temperature reduces yield.

core.h: Grade 9 reasoning: why lowering the barrier matters so much
core.p: Particles in a sample have a spread of energies: a few are very slow, a few are very fast, most are in between. Only those at the high-energy end have enough energy to overcome the activation energy. Lowering the barrier even a little brings a large extra group of particles over the line, so the proportion of successful collisions can rise dramatically. That is why a small amount of catalyst can make a very slow reaction (like hydrogen peroxide decomposing on the shelf) almost instant.
bullets: The particles' energies are **not changed** by the catalyst; the **threshold** is moved down.
The catalyst often works by letting reactants form **temporary bonds or intermediates** on its surface, which breaks the reaction into easier steps; the catalyst is released again at the end.
Because it is regenerated, one catalyst particle can help **many** reactant particles react.
Use the word **proportion** or **percentage** of collisions: this is the most precise way to describe the effect.

callouts.p: 'The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the frequency of successful collisions increases.'

core.p: Exam questions often give you a table of results and ask which substance is a catalyst. A substance is a catalyst only if **two things are true**: it speeds up the reaction **and** its mass (and chemical identity) is unchanged at the end.
bullets: Faster rate but mass decreased: the substance **reacted** (it is a reactant), so it is **not** a catalyst.
No change in rate but mass unchanged: the substance is **not a catalyst** for this reaction (it does nothing).
Faster rate and mass unchanged: it **is** a catalyst.
The best catalyst gives the **largest volume of gas in a set time** or the **shortest time** to collect a fixed volume.
Always compare to a **control** with no catalyst.

callouts.p: Students often pick the substance with the fastest rate without checking whether its mass went down. If it was used up, it is a reactant, not a catalyst.

analogy.p: Imagine cyclists (particles) trying to get from one valley (reactants) to the next valley (products) over a high mountain pass (activation energy). Only the fittest, most energetic cyclists make it over. A catalyst is like digging a **tunnel lower down the mountain**: the cyclists are no fitter than before, but now many more of them have enough energy to get through, so far more reach the other valley each minute. Both valleys stay at the same height, just as the energy change of the reaction is unchanged, and the tunnel is still there afterwards for the next cyclists, just as the catalyst is not used up. Where it breaks down: a real catalyst takes part in the reaction (forming temporary bonds with reactants before being regenerated), whereas a tunnel is just a passive route; and particles do not choose a route, they react via the lower-energy pathway when they meet the catalyst surface.

terms.d: A substance that speeds up the rate of a reaction without altering the products, being itself unchanged chemically and in mass at the end of the reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide for a reaction to occur.
A different route from reactants to products, provided by a catalyst, that has a lower activation energy.
A collision between reactant particles with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, which leads to a reaction.
The number of successful collisions per second; the higher it is, the faster the rate of reaction.
How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed; mean rate = amount of product formed ÷ time taken.
A diagram showing the energy of reactants and products and the activation energy barrier as a reaction progresses.
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products; it is not changed by a catalyst.
A biological catalyst; a protein that speeds up reactions in living things, e.g. enzymes in yeast used in fermentation.
MnO2, a black powder that catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
Iron, used to speed up the reaction of nitrogen and hydrogen to make ammonia.
Vanadium(V) oxide, used to speed up the oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide.
A device in car exhausts containing platinum, palladium and rhodium that catalyses the conversion of harmful gases into less harmful ones.
The same experiment carried out without the catalyst, so the effect of the catalyst can be compared fairly.
A catalyst usually only speeds up one particular reaction or type of reaction.

mistakes.w: A catalyst gives the particles more energy.
mistakes.r: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy; the particles' energy is unchanged.

mistakes.w: A catalyst makes particles collide more often.
mistakes.r: A catalyst increases the proportion of collisions that are successful (frequency of successful collisions), not the total collision frequency.

mistakes.w: A catalyst is used up in the reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst is unchanged chemically and in mass at the end of the reaction.

mistakes.w: A catalyst produces more product.
mistakes.r: A catalyst does not change the amount of product; the reaction just finishes sooner.

mistakes.w: A catalyst lowers the energy needed for the reaction.
mistakes.r: Say it lowers the activation energy (the minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful). 'Energy needed' alone is too vague.

mistakes.w: The catalysed curve on a reaction profile ends at a lower product level.
mistakes.r: Both curves start and end at the same energy levels; only the peak is lower, so the overall energy change is the same.

mistakes.w: A catalyst does not take part in the reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst does take part (e.g. forming temporary intermediates) but is regenerated, so it is unchanged at the end.

mistakes.w: Activation energy is drawn from the products to the top of the curve.
mistakes.r: Activation energy is drawn from the reactants energy level up to the peak of the curve.

mistakes.w: The substance that gave the fastest rate is the catalyst, even though its mass decreased.
mistakes.r: If its mass decreased it reacted, so it is a reactant; a catalyst must also have the same mass at the end.

exam.q: State what is meant by a catalyst.
model: Speeds up / increases the rate of a reaction
Is unchanged (chemically and in mass) at the end of the reaction / not used up
exam.tip: Two marks need two separate ideas: faster rate AND unchanged at the end.

exam.q: Explain how adding a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
model: Catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway
With a lower activation energy
So more particles / a greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ activation energy, so more successful collisions per second
exam.tip: Do not mention particles moving faster or having more energy.

exam.q: Give the meaning of the term activation energy.
model: The minimum energy particles must have when they collide for a reaction to occur
exam.tip: The word 'minimum' is essential.

exam.q: Manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide solution. Write the balanced equation for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
model: Correct formulae: H2O2 → H2O + O2
Balanced: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2
exam.tip: Do not include MnO2 as a reactant or product; it may go over the arrow.

exam.q: Describe how a student could show that the manganese(IV) oxide is not used up in the reaction.
model: Weigh the manganese(IV) oxide before adding it
At the end, filter the mixture, then wash and dry the solid
Reweigh: the mass is the same as at the start
exam.tip: Include filter AND dry; forgetting to dry means water adds mass.

exam.q: A catalyst is added to an exothermic reaction. State the effect on (a) the activation energy and (b) the overall energy change.
model: (a) Activation energy decreases / is lowered
(b) Overall energy change stays the same / is unchanged
exam.tip: Remember: hump lower, levels unchanged.

exam.q: Draw a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction with and without a catalyst. Label the activation energy for the catalysed reaction.
model: Products drawn at a lower energy level than reactants
Two humps: catalysed curve has a lower peak, both curves start and finish at the same levels
Activation energy arrow drawn from reactants level to the peak of the catalysed curve and labelled
exam.tip: Use a ruler for the levels and arrows and label axes: energy and progress of reaction.

exam.q: The volume of oxygen produced when hydrogen peroxide decomposes was measured with and without a catalyst. Describe and explain how the graph for the catalysed reaction differs from the uncatalysed reaction.
model: Catalysed curve is steeper at the start / higher initial rate
Levels off sooner / reaction finishes earlier
Same final volume of oxygen
Because the catalyst lowers activation energy but does not change the amount of product / same amount of hydrogen peroxide used up
exam.tip: Describe first (shape), then explain (why).

exam.q: Give two reasons why catalysts are used in industrial processes such as the Haber process.
model: Products are made faster / increase rate, so more product per day
Allows lower temperatures to be used, saving energy / fuel / money / less CO2 released; catalyst is not used up so can be reused
exam.tip: Link to cost and energy: 'cheaper' alone is often not enough, say why it is cheaper.

exam.q: A student investigates the effectiveness of three metal oxides as catalysts for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Describe a method the student could use, including how to make it a fair test.
model: Measure a fixed volume (e.g. 25 cm³) of hydrogen peroxide of the same concentration into a conical flask
Add a fixed mass (e.g. 0.5 g) of the first metal oxide as a powder
Immediately connect a gas syringe / upturned measuring cylinder in water and start a stopwatch
Record the volume of oxygen every 10 s (or the volume after a fixed time)
Repeat with the other oxides and with no catalyst as a control
Keep temperature, volume and concentration of H2O2, mass and particle size of oxide the same
Largest volume of gas in a set time / steepest graph = most effective catalyst
Filter, dry and reweigh each oxide to check its mass is unchanged
exam.tip: A level 3 answer is a logical, step-by-step method with measurements, control variables and how to decide the result.

worked.q: Students added 0.50 g of four solids, A to D, to 25 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide. Volume of O2 after 60 s: none 2 cm³, A 2 cm³, B 48 cm³, C 30 cm³, D 55 cm³. Mass recovered: A 0.50 g, B 0.50 g, C 0.50 g, D 0.31 g. Which solid is the best catalyst?
steps: A catalyst must speed up the reaction AND be unchanged in mass.
A: 2 cm³ is the same as no solid, so A does not speed up the reaction. Not a catalyst.
D: fastest (55 cm³), but its mass fell from 0.50 g to 0.31 g, so it was used up: it reacted, so it is not a catalyst.
B and C: both faster than the control and mass unchanged, so both are catalysts.
B produced more oxygen in 60 s (48 cm³ vs 30 cm³), so B gives the higher rate.
worked.ans: B is the best catalyst: it gives the highest rate of the solids whose mass is unchanged. D is not a catalyst because it was used up.

worked.q: Without a catalyst, 50 cm³ of oxygen is collected in 200 s. With a catalyst, the same 50 cm³ is collected in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate in each case and state how many times faster the catalysed reaction is. State the final volume of oxygen if the reaction runs to completion in each case.
steps: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time.
Uncatalysed: 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25 cm³/s.
Catalysed: 50 ÷ 40 = 1.25 cm³/s.
1.25 ÷ 0.25 = 5, so the catalysed reaction is 5 times faster.
The catalyst does not change the amount of product, so the final volume of oxygen at completion is the same in both cases.
worked.ans: 0.25 cm³/s without and 1.25 cm³/s with the catalyst (5 times faster); the final volume of oxygen is the same in both.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain, in terms of particles and energy, why adding iron to the Haber process increases the rate at which ammonia is made, and why the amount of energy released per mole of ammonia stays the same.
steps: Iron is a catalyst: it provides an alternative reaction pathway for nitrogen and hydrogen to react.
This pathway has a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed reaction.
The gas particles have the same range of energies as before, but a greater proportion of them now have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
So a greater proportion of collisions are successful and the frequency of successful collisions increases: the rate increases.
The energy levels of the reactants (N2 and H2) and the product (NH3) are not changed by the catalyst, so the overall energy change is the same.
worked.ans: The iron catalyst lowers the activation energy via an alternative pathway, increasing the frequency of successful collisions; it does not change the energy of reactants or products, so the overall energy change is unchanged.

chem_edx.7.5.summary: **Enzymes are biological catalysts**: proteins made by living cells that speed up chemical reactions without being used up. The key industrial example on the Edexcel specification is the use of **enzymes in yeast** to make **alcoholic drinks** by **fermentation**, in which glucose is converted into **ethanol and carbon dioxide** under **anaerobic** conditions at a warm temperature. Grade 9 answers explain why the conditions are chosen: enzymes work fastest at an **optimum temperature and pH**, and are **denatured** if it is too hot.

core.p: A catalyst speeds up the rate of a reaction without altering the products and is itself unchanged chemically and in mass at the end. **Enzymes** do exactly the same job, but they are made by living organisms. Every living cell relies on thousands of enzymes to make reactions such as respiration and digestion happen fast enough at body temperature.
bullets: Enzymes are **biological catalysts**: catalysts made by living things.
Enzymes are **proteins** (large molecules made of chains of amino acids folded into a specific shape).
Like all catalysts, enzymes **speed up reactions** and are **not used up**.
Like all catalysts, they work by providing an **alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy**.
Enzymes let reactions happen quickly at **low, mild temperatures** (e.g. 37 °C in the body) and normal pressure.
The Edexcel spec point to recall: enzymes are biological catalysts and **enzymes are used in the production of alcoholic drinks**.

callouts.p: A biological catalyst: a protein produced by living cells that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.

core.h: How enzymes work: the active site
core.p: Each enzyme has a specially shaped region called the **active site**. Only a reactant molecule (the **substrate**) with the complementary shape can fit into it. This is often described with the **lock and key** model: the substrate is the key and the active site is the lock. When the substrate binds, bonds in it are strained or brought into the right position, so the reaction needs less energy: the **activation energy is lowered**. The products are released and the active site is free to be used again.
bullets: Substrate binds to the **active site**, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The reaction happens with a **lower activation energy**.
Products leave the active site; the **enzyme is unchanged** and can catalyse again.
Enzymes are **specific**: each enzyme usually catalyses only **one reaction** or one type of reaction, because only one substrate shape fits.
One enzyme molecule can catalyse **thousands of reactions per second**, so only small amounts are needed.

callouts.p: Enzymes increase rate in exactly the same way as other catalysts: an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

fig.cap: Lock and key model. The substrate fits the complementary shape of the enzyme's active site; it is broken into products, which leave. The enzyme is unchanged and can be reused.

core.p: Enzyme-catalysed reactions speed up as temperature rises, because particles move faster and collide more often and with more energy. But above a certain temperature the rate falls sharply. This is because the enzyme is a protein: too much heat makes its molecule vibrate so much that the bonds holding its shape break, the **active site changes shape**, and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme is **denatured**. Denaturing is **permanent**; cooling does not reverse it.
bullets: Rate increases with temperature up to the **optimum temperature** (fastest rate).
Above the optimum, the enzyme is **denatured**: the active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits.
Human enzymes have an optimum of about **37 °C**.
Enzymes in yeast used for fermentation work best at about **30-35 °C** (warm, not hot).
At low temperatures enzymes are **not denatured**, just **slow** (fewer, lower-energy collisions); warming them up restores activity.
This is a key difference from most inorganic catalysts (such as iron or platinum), which work well at high temperatures.

callouts.p: Enzymes are molecules, not living things, so they are denatured, not killed. (Yeast cells, which are alive, can be killed.)

core.p: Each enzyme also has an **optimum pH**. If the pH is too acidic or too alkaline, the charges and bonds that hold the active site's shape are disrupted, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is **denatured**. Most enzymes, including those in yeast, work best near **neutral to slightly acidic** pH.
bullets: Rate is highest at the **optimum pH**.
Far from the optimum, the **active site changes shape** and the enzyme is denatured.
Different enzymes have different optimum pH values (e.g. stomach enzymes work in acid).
In fermentation, the solution must not become too acidic, or the yeast enzymes slow down.

core.p: Alcoholic drinks contain **ethanol**, C2H5OH. It is made by **fermentation**: **yeast**, a single-celled fungus, is added to a solution of sugar (such as glucose) in water. **Enzymes in the yeast** catalyse the conversion of glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The yeast does this to release energy when there is **no oxygen** (anaerobic respiration).
bullets: Word equation: **glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide**.
Balanced symbol equation: **C6H12O6(aq) → 2C2H5OH(aq) + 2CO2(g)**.
The **enzymes in yeast** are the catalyst (written over the arrow, not as a reactant).
Conditions: **anaerobic** (air/oxygen excluded), **warm (about 30-35 °C)**, sugar **dissolved in water**, suitable pH.
The **carbon dioxide** produced makes beer and sparkling wine fizzy, and makes bread dough rise in baking.
The CO2 bubbles can be tested with **limewater**, which turns **milky / cloudy**.

callouts.p: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2. Check: 6 C, 12 H and 6 O on each side.

fig.cap: Fermentation apparatus. Yeast and sugar solution are kept warm (about 30-35 °C) in a flask fitted with a delivery tube or airlock. Carbon dioxide escapes and turns limewater milky, but air cannot get in, keeping conditions anaerobic.

core.h: Why each fermentation condition is chosen
core.p: Every condition in fermentation is there to keep the yeast enzymes working at a good rate and to stop unwanted side reactions. Explaining the reason for each condition is a favourite 4-mark question.
bullets: **Warm (about 30-35 °C)**: fast enough rate; enzymes are near their optimum temperature.
**Not too hot**: above about 40 °C the enzymes are **denatured** (and the yeast is killed), so fermentation stops.
**Not too cold**: the reaction is very **slow** (enzymes not denatured, just slow).
**Anaerobic (no air)**: if oxygen gets in, the yeast respires aerobically making CO2 and water instead of ethanol, and microbes can **oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid** (vinegar), spoiling the drink.
An **airlock** lets carbon dioxide out but stops air getting in.
**Sugar in solution** (water): the enzymes and glucose must be dissolved for particles to collide.
Fermentation slows and stops when the sugar is used up, or when the ethanol concentration reaches about **15%**, because ethanol becomes toxic to the yeast.

head: Condition
Reason
rows: Stops ethanol being oxidised to ethanoic acid; yeast makes ethanol, not CO2 and water
Sugar and enzymes dissolved so they can collide

callouts.p: For 'explain why the temperature is kept at 35 °C', give both sides: lower would be too slow; higher would denature the enzymes.

core.p: All alcoholic drinks are made by fermentation, but the sugar source differs. The flavour comes from the plant material used. Fermentation alone can only reach about 15% ethanol, so stronger drinks (spirits) need an extra step: **fractional distillation**, which separates ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) from water (100 °C) to make a more concentrated solution.
bullets: **Wine**: fermentation of sugars in **grape** juice.
**Beer**: fermentation of sugars from **barley** (malted grain); in malting, enzymes break down **starch** into sugars that yeast can ferment.
**Cider**: fermentation of **apple** juice.
**Spirits** (whisky, vodka): fermented liquid is **fractionally distilled** to increase the ethanol concentration.
After fermentation the yeast is removed by **filtration** or allowed to settle.
The same reaction is used to make ethanol as a **biofuel**.

core.p: Enzymes and industrial catalysts (such as iron in the Haber process) both lower activation energy and are not used up, but their properties differ because enzymes are proteins.
bullets: Enzymes work at **low temperatures and normal pressure**, saving energy.
Enzymes are **very specific**; many inorganic catalysts can catalyse several reactions.
Enzymes are **denatured** by high temperatures and extreme pH; metal catalysts are not.
Enzymes come from **renewable** living sources and are **biodegradable**.
Enzyme processes are usually **slower** and are often batch processes.

core.p: Enzymes are widely used because they let reactions happen at mild conditions. Knowing a few examples helps in 'evaluate' or 'suggest' questions, though the spec specifically names alcoholic drinks.
bullets: **Baking**: yeast enzymes produce CO2 that makes bread rise (the ethanol evaporates during baking).
**Biological washing powders**: enzymes break down stains at low washing temperatures, saving energy.
**Digestion**: amylase, protease and lipase break down food molecules in the body.
**Food industry**: enzymes convert starch into sugar syrups.

callouts.p: They work best in cool washes; a very hot wash denatures the enzymes, so they stop working.

core.p: You can follow the rate of fermentation by measuring the **carbon dioxide** produced: count the **bubbles per minute** through the airlock or limewater, collect the gas in a **gas syringe**, or measure the **loss of mass** as CO2 escapes. Repeating at different temperatures in water baths shows the optimum temperature.
bullets: Independent variable: e.g. **temperature** of the water bath.
Dependent variable: **volume of CO2** (or bubbles per minute, or mass lost) in a set time.
Control variables: **mass of yeast**, **concentration and volume of sugar solution**, pH, time.
Allow the mixture to reach the water bath temperature before starting.
Counting bubbles is less accurate (bubbles vary in size); a gas syringe gives more precise results.

core.p: The best answers connect the enzyme spec point with collision theory and activation energy. Raising the temperature from cold to warm increases rate because particles move faster and collide more frequently with more energy. Enzymes lower the activation energy so this happens at a useful rate at only 30-35 °C. But because the enzyme is a protein, there is a limit: above the optimum the active site loses its shape, so substrate molecules can no longer bind and the rate drops, even though particles are moving faster.
bullets: Below optimum: rate limited by **collision frequency and energy**.
Above optimum: rate limited by the **number of working active sites** (enzymes denatured).
Using enzymes means **less energy** is needed for heating, which is cheaper and releases less CO2 from burning fuels.
Fermentation uses **renewable** sugar from crops, unlike making ethanol from crude oil (hydration of ethene).

analogy.t: A key-cutting machine in a workshop
analogy.p: Think of an enzyme as a precision machine with a uniquely shaped slot (the active site). Only one type of blank (the substrate) fits the slot, and once it is in, the machine makes the job much easier than doing it by hand (lower activation energy). The finished pieces (products) drop out and the machine is ready for the next blank: it is not used up. Warming the workshop makes the workers deliver blanks faster, but if it gets too hot the machine's slot warps and no blank fits any more (denatured), and it cannot be repaired by cooling down. Where it breaks down: a real enzyme is not rigid; its active site can flex slightly around the substrate, and nobody 'feeds' it: substrate molecules arrive by random collisions.

terms.d: A biological catalyst; a protein made by living cells that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
A catalyst produced by a living organism, i.e. an enzyme.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without altering the products, being unchanged chemically and in mass at the end.
The region of an enzyme with a specific shape where the substrate binds and the reaction is catalysed.
The reactant molecule that binds to an enzyme's active site.
The model in which the substrate fits the complementary shape of the active site, like a key fits a lock.
An enzyme usually only catalyses one reaction, because only one substrate fits its active site.
The temperature at which an enzyme-catalysed reaction is fastest.
The pH at which an enzyme-catalysed reaction is fastest.
When an enzyme's active site permanently changes shape (due to high temperature or extreme pH) so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme stops working.
The conversion of sugars such as glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide by enzymes in yeast under anaerobic conditions.
A single-celled fungus whose enzymes catalyse fermentation.
Without oxygen; fermentation must be anaerobic so ethanol is produced and not oxidised.
C2H5OH, the alcohol in alcoholic drinks, produced by fermentation.
A valve on a fermentation vessel that lets carbon dioxide out but stops air getting in.
Separation of liquids by boiling point; used to concentrate ethanol from fermented liquid to make spirits.

exam.tip: Use the exact phrase 'biological catalysts'.

Enzymes in yeast catalyse conversion of glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide
Equation: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2
Temperature about 30-35 °C: fast rate, near optimum for enzymes
Not too hot or enzymes are denatured

exam.tip: Level 3: a full description linked to clear reasons for each condition.

worked.q: A student measured the volume of CO2 produced by fermentation in 10 minutes at different temperatures: 15 °C 6 cm³, 25 °C 14 cm³, 35 °C 24 cm³, 45 °C 9 cm³, 55 °C 0 cm³. Describe and explain the results and find the mean rate at 35 °C.
steps: From 15 °C to 35 °C the volume of CO2 increases: particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent and more have energy ≥ activation energy.
The highest volume is at 35 °C, so the optimum is around 35 °C (somewhere between 25 °C and 45 °C).
Above 35 °C the volume falls, and at 55 °C no CO2 is made: the enzymes are denatured, the active site changes shape, so glucose no longer fits.
Mean rate at 35 °C = 24 cm³ ÷ 10 min = 2.4 cm³/min (or 24 ÷ 600 s = 0.04 cm³/s).
worked.ans: Rate rises to an optimum near 35 °C then falls as enzymes are denatured; mean rate at 35 °C = 2.4 cm³/min.

worked.q: Show that the fermentation equation C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 is balanced, and calculate the mass of ethanol formed from 180 g of glucose (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16).
steps: Left: C 6, H 12, O 6.
Right: 2C2H5OH gives C 4, H 12, O 2; 2CO2 gives C 2, O 4. Total C 6, H 12, O 6. Balanced.
1 mol glucose makes 2 mol ethanol. Mr ethanol = (2 × 12) + (6 × 1) + 16 = 46.
Mass of ethanol = 2 × 46 = 92 g.
worked.ans: The equation is balanced; 180 g of glucose produces 92 g of ethanol.

worked.q: Model answer: A winemaker leaves the airlock off and keeps the barrel next to a hot boiler at 50 °C. Explain two problems.
steps: Without the airlock, air (oxygen) can enter the barrel.
Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid, so the wine turns sour (vinegar) and less ethanol is made.
At 50 °C, which is well above the optimum of about 30-35 °C, the enzymes in yeast are denatured: the active site changes shape so glucose no longer fits.
So fermentation slows or stops and little ethanol is produced.
worked.ans: Oxygen gets in and ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid; the high temperature denatures the yeast enzymes so fermentation stops.

chem_edx.7.6.summary: Chemical reactions and some physical changes are accompanied by **heat energy changes**, which show up as a **temperature rise or fall** of the surroundings. Edexcel names four types to know: **salts dissolving in water, neutralisation, displacement and precipitation**, and a **core practical** to investigate their temperature changes using a polystyrene cup and thermometer. An **exothermic** change gives out heat energy to the surroundings, so the temperature **rises**; an **endothermic** change takes in heat energy from the surroundings, so the temperature **falls**.

core.p: Whenever a chemical reaction happens, energy is transferred between the **reacting chemicals (the system)** and the **surroundings** (the water the chemicals are dissolved in, the container, the air, a thermometer). Energy is **conserved**: it is never created or destroyed, only transferred. If energy moves out of the chemicals, the surroundings get hotter. If energy moves into the chemicals, the surroundings get colder.
bullets: Changes in **heat energy** accompany: **salts dissolving in water**, **neutralisation reactions**, **displacement reactions** and **precipitation reactions**.
These changes can result in a **rise or a fall in temperature**.
The thermometer measures the temperature of the **surroundings** (mainly the water/solution), not the energy stored in the chemicals.
The **size** of the temperature change depends on how much energy is transferred and how much substance (e.g. water) is being heated or cooled.
Energy is **conserved**: energy given out by the reaction = energy gained by the surroundings.

callouts.p: In every reaction the total energy of the chemicals plus the surroundings stays the same; energy is only transferred between them.

core.p: An **exothermic** change or reaction is one in which **heat energy is given out to the surroundings**. Because the surroundings gain energy, their **temperature increases**. The products end up with **less stored chemical energy** than the reactants: the difference has been released as heat.
bullets: Heat energy is **transferred from the reacting chemicals to the surroundings**.
Temperature of the surroundings **rises**; the reaction mixture feels **hot**.
Overall energy change is **negative** (energy lost by the chemicals): ΔH is negative.
Examples: **combustion**, **neutralisation** (acid + alkali), **displacement** reactions (e.g. zinc + copper(II) sulfate), **respiration**, reactions of metals with acids, **oxidation** reactions.
Some **salts dissolving** are exothermic, e.g. anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, calcium chloride, sodium hydroxide (strictly a base, but dissolves exothermically).
Many **precipitation** reactions give a small temperature rise.

callouts.p: A change or reaction in which heat energy is given out to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.

core.p: An **endothermic** change or reaction is one in which **heat energy is taken in from the surroundings**. Because the surroundings lose energy, their **temperature decreases**. The products end up with **more stored chemical energy** than the reactants.
bullets: Heat energy is **transferred from the surroundings to the reacting chemicals**.
Temperature of the surroundings **falls**; the mixture feels **cold**.
Overall energy change is **positive** (energy gained by the chemicals): ΔH is positive.

Examples: **dissolving ammonium nitrate** or **ammonium chloride** in water, **thermal decomposition** (e.g. calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide), reaction of **citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate**, **ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate**, **photosynthesis**.
Endothermic reactions often need **continuous heating** to keep them going (e.g. thermal decomposition).

callouts.p: A change or reaction in which heat energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
An endothermic reaction feels cold because it takes energy FROM your hand (the surroundings). It is not 'releasing cold'.

core.h: The four named types of change
core.p: Edexcel specifically names four types of change whose temperature changes you should recall and be able to investigate. Some are always exothermic; others can go either way depending on the substances.
bullets: **Salts dissolving in water**: can be **endothermic** (ammonium nitrate, ammonium chloride, potassium nitrate) or **exothermic** (anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, calcium chloride).
**Neutralisation** (acid + alkali → salt + water): **exothermic**, e.g. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. Ionic equation: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l).

**Displacement** (more reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from a solution of its salt): **exothermic**, e.g. Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu. The further apart the metals in the reactivity series, the bigger the temperature rise.
**Precipitation** (two solutions react to form an insoluble solid): usually a **small** temperature change, often a slight rise, e.g. AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO3, or BaCl2 + Na2SO4 → BaSO4 + 2NaCl.
Exception to know: the reaction of **sodium hydrogencarbonate with citric acid or ethanoic acid** is endothermic, even though it is an acid reaction (it is not a simple alkali neutralisation).

callouts.p: Dissolving a salt is a physical change, so call it an exothermic or endothermic 'change' or 'process', not a reaction.

core.p: In the core practical you mix reactants in an insulated container and measure the temperature change. A **polystyrene cup** is used because polystyrene is a good **thermal insulator**, so less heat is lost to (or gained from) the air, and it has a low heat capacity so it absorbs little energy itself. The cup is stood in a **beaker** to stop it falling over, and a **lid** reduces heat loss by evaporation and convection.
bullets: Measure a known volume (e.g. **25 cm³**) of solution or water into a polystyrene cup with a **measuring cylinder**.
Stand the cup in a beaker for stability; put the **thermometer** in and record the **initial temperature** once it is steady.
Add the second reactant: a measured volume of solution, or a weighed mass of solid (e.g. **1 g** of salt, or an **excess of metal powder** for displacement).
Put the **lid** on, **stir** with the thermometer (or a stirrer) and record the **highest** temperature (exothermic) or **lowest** temperature (endothermic) reached.
Temperature change = final temperature - initial temperature. Positive = rise = exothermic; negative = fall = endothermic.
**Repeat** and calculate a mean; discard anomalous results.
Control variables: **volume and concentration** of solutions, **mass and particle size** of solid, **starting temperature**, type of cup and lid.

callouts.p: Heat is lost to the surroundings (air, thermometer) even with a lid, so the measured temperature rise is usually smaller than the true value. Use a lid, insulation and stir so the reading is the true maximum.

core.h: Following a neutralisation with a temperature graph
core.p: A common extension is to add an alkali to a fixed volume of acid in small portions (e.g. 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide at a time into 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid) and record the temperature after each addition. The temperature **rises** while neutralisation is happening, reaches a **maximum** when the acid has just been **exactly neutralised**, then **falls** as extra alkali is added.
bullets: Rising section: each portion of alkali reacts with acid, releasing heat (exothermic).
Maximum: all the acid has been neutralised; no more reaction can occur.
Falling section: the excess alkali added is at room temperature and does not react, so it **cools** the mixture, and heat is also lost to the surroundings.
Draw **two straight lines of best fit** (rising and falling); where they cross gives the **volume of alkali needed to neutralise** the acid and the true maximum temperature.
A larger concentration of acid and alkali gives a **bigger temperature rise**, because more particles react in the same volume of solution.

core.p: In data questions you decide from the sign of the temperature change. Always compare the final temperature with the starting temperature of the solution, not with room temperature.
bullets: Final temperature **higher** than initial: heat given out: **exothermic**.
Final temperature **lower** than initial: heat taken in: **endothermic**.
Temperature change = final - initial (keep the sign: e.g. -4.5 °C).
A **larger** temperature change (with the same volume of solution) means **more heat energy** transferred.
For displacement, compare metals: e.g. magnesium gives a bigger rise with copper(II) sulfate than zinc does, because magnesium is further above copper in the reactivity series.
Over time, the mixture returns to room temperature as heat is transferred between it and the room.

callouts.p: Record temperatures to the precision of the thermometer (e.g. 0.5 °C) and keep the same number of decimal places throughout a table.

core.h: Why: energy stored in chemical bonds (link to 7.12-7.14)
core.p: Whether a change is exothermic or endothermic depends on the balance between energy taken in to **break bonds** and energy released when **new bonds form**. Breaking bonds always needs energy (endothermic); making bonds always releases energy (exothermic). If more energy is released making bonds than is needed to break bonds, the reaction is **exothermic** overall. If more energy is needed to break bonds than is released making them, it is **endothermic** overall. This is the reason behind the temperature changes, and it is covered fully in spec points 7.12-7.14.
bullets: Exothermic overall: energy released making bonds **>** energy taken in breaking bonds.
Endothermic overall: energy taken in breaking bonds **>** energy released making bonds.
On a reaction profile, exothermic: products **lower** than reactants; endothermic: products **higher** (spec 7.15-7.16).

core.h: Everyday uses of exothermic and endothermic changes
core.p: Temperature changes from reactions are put to practical use. Examiners often ask you to suggest which reaction suits a device, or to evaluate one.
bullets: **Hand warmers** (exothermic): oxidation of iron powder, or crystallisation of a supersaturated sodium ethanoate solution (reusable).
**Self-heating cans** of food or coffee (exothermic): e.g. calcium oxide reacting with water.
**Instant cold packs** for sports injuries (endothermic): ammonium nitrate dissolving in water when an inner bag is broken.
**Sherbet** feels cool on the tongue: citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate reaction is endothermic.
Combustion of fuels (exothermic) to heat homes and power vehicles.
Disposable packs work once; reusable packs use a reversible change and can be reset.

core.p: Six-mark questions often ask you to evaluate or improve the method. The biggest problem is **heat transfer to or from the surroundings**, which makes the measured temperature change smaller than it should be.
bullets: Use a **lid** and **extra insulation** (e.g. a second cup or cotton wool) to reduce heat loss.
**Stir** so the mixture is the same temperature throughout and the thermometer shows the true maximum/minimum.
Use a **digital thermometer / temperature probe** with higher resolution (e.g. 0.1 °C) and a data logger.
Make sure both solutions start at the **same temperature** before mixing.
Use a **powder** for solids so the reaction is fast and the maximum is reached before much heat is lost.
**Repeat** and calculate a mean to improve reliability; use a **pipette or burette** for more accurate volumes.

callouts.p: Wear eye protection: acids, alkalis, copper(II) sulfate and silver nitrate are irritants or harmful; avoid skin contact with silver nitrate.

analogy.t: A bank account and its neighbour
analogy.p: Think of the reacting chemicals as one bank account and the surroundings as the account next door; heat energy is the money. In an **exothermic** change the chemicals pay money out to the surroundings, so the surroundings get richer (hotter), just as the temperature reading rises. In an **endothermic** change the chemicals take money from the surroundings, so the surroundings get poorer (colder). The total money in both accounts never changes, just as energy is conserved. Where it breaks down: the thermometer only 'sees' the surroundings' account, and in a real experiment some money leaks to a third account (the air and the cup), so the measured change is smaller than the true one; also chemical energy is stored in bonds, not as a single pot of coins.

terms.d: A change or reaction in which heat energy is given out to the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
A change or reaction in which heat energy is taken in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls.
Everything other than the reacting chemicals, e.g. the water, container, thermometer and air.
The reacting chemicals themselves.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred; the total energy before and after a reaction is the same.
Reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to form a salt and water; exothermic.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt; exothermic.
A reaction between two solutions that forms an insoluble solid (a precipitate).
A physical change in which a solute spreads through a solvent to form a solution; can be exothermic or endothermic.
Final temperature minus initial temperature; positive for exothermic, negative for endothermic.
A material, such as polystyrene, that reduces the transfer of heat energy.
Insulated container used in the core practical to reduce heat transfer to or from the surroundings.
Breaking down a substance using heat, e.g. calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide; endothermic.
Energy transferred between chemicals and surroundings; negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.
Transfer of heat from the mixture to the air and apparatus, which makes measured temperature changes smaller than the true value.

mistakes.w: An endothermic reaction gives out cold.
mistakes.r: An endothermic reaction takes in heat energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.

mistakes.w: Exothermic reactions take in heat.
mistakes.r: Exothermic reactions give out heat energy to the surroundings (exo = out).

mistakes.w: The temperature fell, so the reaction is exothermic.
mistakes.r: A fall in temperature means heat was taken in: endothermic.

mistakes.w: Energy is used up / created in the reaction.
mistakes.r: Energy is conserved; it is transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings.

mistakes.w: The polystyrene cup is used because it does not react / is cheap.
mistakes.r: Polystyrene is a good thermal insulator, so it reduces heat loss to (or gain from) the surroundings.

mistakes.w: All salts dissolving are endothermic.
mistakes.r: Some are endothermic (e.g. ammonium nitrate) and some are exothermic (e.g. anhydrous copper(II) sulfate).

mistakes.w: The lid is used to stop the solution spilling.
mistakes.r: The lid reduces heat loss to the surroundings (by convection/evaporation).

mistakes.w: Temperature after the reaction finishes is the result.
mistakes.r: Record the maximum (or minimum) temperature reached, then calculate the change from the initial temperature.

mistakes.w: In an exothermic reaction the products have more energy than the reactants.
mistakes.r: In an exothermic reaction the products have less energy than the reactants; the difference is released as heat.

exam.q: What is meant by an exothermic reaction?
model: A reaction in which heat energy is given out / transferred to the surroundings (so temperature rises)
exam.tip: Mention the surroundings.

exam.q: State what happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an endothermic change.
model: It decreases / falls
exam.tip: Endo = in: heat goes into the chemicals from the surroundings.

exam.q: When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, the temperature falls from 21.0 °C to 14.5 °C. Calculate the temperature change and state whether the change is exothermic or endothermic.
model: Temperature change = 14.5 - 21.0 = -6.5 °C (fall of 6.5 °C)
Endothermic
exam.tip: Show the subtraction and keep the sign.

exam.q: Name two types of reaction that are exothermic.
model: Neutralisation
Displacement / combustion / oxidation / respiration
exam.tip: Any two correct; neutralisation and displacement are the spec examples.

exam.q: Explain why a polystyrene cup with a lid is used when measuring temperature changes in reactions.
model: Polystyrene is a (good) thermal insulator
Lid and cup reduce heat loss to the surroundings, so the temperature change measured is more accurate
exam.tip: 'Insulator' is the key word.

exam.q: Zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and the temperature rises by 8 °C. Magnesium powder gives a rise of 25 °C. Explain the difference.
model: Magnesium is more reactive than zinc / further from copper in the reactivity series
So more heat energy is released (bigger temperature rise)
exam.tip: Link reactivity to the size of energy release.

exam.q: Give one use of an endothermic change and one use of an exothermic change.
model: Endothermic: instant cold pack for sports injuries (ammonium nitrate dissolving)
Exothermic: hand warmer / self-heating can
exam.tip: Name both the device and its type.

exam.q: A student adds 5 cm³ portions of sodium hydroxide to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid and records the temperature. Explain why the temperature rises and then falls.
model: Neutralisation is exothermic, so temperature rises as alkali reacts with acid
Maximum temperature when all the acid has been neutralised
Then excess (cooler) alkali added does not react, so it cools the mixture / heat lost to surroundings
exam.tip: Explain each section of the graph separately.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of energy transfer, why the temperature of the solution increases during a neutralisation reaction.
model: Energy (heat) is transferred from the reacting chemicals
To the surroundings / the water in the solution, so its temperature increases
exam.tip: The solution is the surroundings.

exam.q: Describe how you would carry out an experiment to find whether dissolving a salt in water is exothermic or endothermic. Include how you would make the results valid and how you would interpret them.
model: Measure 25 cm³ of water with a measuring cylinder into a polystyrene cup in a beaker
Record the initial temperature with a thermometer
Add a measured mass (e.g. 2 g) of the salt and put on a lid
Stir and record the highest or lowest temperature reached
Calculate the temperature change = final - initial
Repeat and find a mean; keep volume of water, mass of salt and starting temperature the same
Temperature rise means exothermic; temperature fall means endothermic
Insulation and lid reduce heat transfer with the surroundings
exam.tip: Level 3 needs a full sequence with measurements, controls and interpretation.

exam.q: Evaluate the student's method in which a glass beaker without a lid was used to measure the temperature change of a displacement reaction.
model: Glass is a conductor of heat / beaker not insulated, so heat lost to surroundings
No lid, so more heat lost by convection / evaporation
So the measured temperature rise is smaller than the true value
Improve by using a polystyrene cup with a lid, stirring, and repeating
exam.tip: Evaluate = identify weakness, effect on result, and improvement.

worked.q: A student mixes 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid at 19.5 °C with 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution at 19.5 °C. The highest temperature reached is 26.0 °C. Three repeats give temperature rises of 6.5 °C, 6.0 °C and 9.5 °C. Calculate the mean temperature rise and decide whether the reaction is exothermic.
steps: First run: 26.0 - 19.5 = 6.5 °C rise.
9.5 °C is anomalous (very different from the others), so ignore it.
The temperature rose, so heat energy was given out to the surroundings.
worked.ans: Mean rise = 6.3 °C (ignoring the anomalous 9.5 °C); the reaction is exothermic.

worked.q: Results: potassium nitrate dissolving: start 20.0 °C, end 16.5 °C. Calcium chloride dissolving: start 20.0 °C, end 31.0 °C. Classify each change and identify which transfers more heat energy (same volume of water used).
steps: Potassium nitrate: 16.5 - 20.0 = -3.5 °C, a fall, so endothermic.
Calcium chloride: 31.0 - 20.0 = +11.0 °C, a rise, so exothermic.
Same volume of water, so the bigger size of temperature change shows more energy transferred: 11.0 °C is bigger than 3.5 °C.
worked.ans: Potassium nitrate dissolving is endothermic (-3.5 °C); calcium chloride dissolving is exothermic (+11.0 °C) and transfers more heat energy.

worked.q: Model answer: A company wants a self-heating can of soup. Which would they choose: ammonium nitrate + water, or calcium oxide + water? Explain.
steps: The can must heat the soup, so the reaction must transfer heat energy to the surroundings (the soup).
This needs an exothermic change, where the temperature of the surroundings rises.
Ammonium nitrate dissolving is endothermic: it takes in heat, so it would cool the soup.
Calcium oxide reacting with water is exothermic, releasing heat to the soup.
worked.ans: Calcium oxide + water, because it is exothermic and gives out heat to the soup; ammonium nitrate dissolving is endothermic and would cool it (suited to a cold pack).

chem_edx.7.7.summary: Every chemical reaction involves **breaking bonds** in the reactants and **making new bonds** in the products. Breaking bonds is always **endothermic** (energy is taken in) and making bonds is always **exothermic** (energy is released). Whether a whole reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on which of these two energy totals is bigger, and at Higher tier you must calculate the overall energy change from **bond energies** in kJ mol-1 using: energy change = energy taken in to break bonds - energy released making bonds.

core.h: Reactions rearrange atoms by breaking and making bonds
core.p: In a chemical reaction the atoms themselves are not created or destroyed. Instead, the **bonds holding the reactant atoms together are broken** and the atoms are rearranged and joined by **new bonds** to make the products. Every reaction therefore has two energy steps: an energy cost and an energy payback.
bullets: Reactant molecules must be pulled apart into separate atoms (in theory) before new bonds can form.
Example: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl. The H-H bond and the Cl-Cl bond are broken, then two H-Cl bonds are made.
The total number of each type of atom is the same on both sides; only the bonding changes.
The overall energy change of the reaction is the **difference** between the energy used to break bonds and the energy released when new bonds form.
This idea explains why some reactions heat the surroundings (exothermic) and some cool them (endothermic).

callouts.p: Step 1: break bonds in reactants (energy in). Step 2: make bonds in products (energy out).

core.p: A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the two bonded atoms. To separate the atoms you must do work against this attraction, so **energy must be supplied**. Breaking a bond therefore **takes in energy from the surroundings**, which makes bond breaking an **endothermic** process.
bullets: Breaking bonds **always** requires energy - there are no exceptions.
The energy is taken in from the surroundings (usually as heat).
The stronger the bond, the more energy is needed to break it.
Double and triple bonds (such as O=O and N≡N) need more energy to break than single bonds between the same atoms because more shared electron pairs hold the atoms together.
Students often wrongly say breaking bonds releases energy - it never does.

callouts.p: Breaking bonds is an endothermic process: energy is taken in (absorbed) from the surroundings.
Food and fuels do NOT release energy because their bonds break. Energy is released because the new bonds made in the products release more energy than was needed to break the old ones.

core.p: When two atoms come together and form a covalent bond, the electrons and nuclei become attracted to each other and the system moves to a **lower, more stable energy state**. The energy lost by the atoms is **released to the surroundings**, usually as heat. So **making bonds is exothermic**.
bullets: Making bonds **always** releases energy.
The energy released when a bond forms is **exactly equal** to the energy needed to break that same bond.
Example: breaking 1 mol of H-H bonds takes in 436 kJ; making 1 mol of H-H bonds gives out 436 kJ.
The stronger the new bond formed, the more energy is released.
The released energy warms the surroundings, so the temperature of a reaction mixture goes up if bond making dominates.

Type
Sign of energy term

callouts.p: Making bonds is an exothermic process: energy is released (given out) to the surroundings.

core.p: A reaction is **exothermic overall** when **more heat energy is released forming new bonds in the products than is needed to break the bonds in the reactants**. The extra energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
bullets: Energy released (making bonds) > energy taken in (breaking bonds).
The overall energy change, ΔH, is **negative**.
The products are at a **lower energy** than the reactants on an energy diagram.
Examples: combustion of fuels such as methane, neutralisation, the reaction of hydrogen with chlorine or oxygen.
The products usually have stronger (or more) bonds overall than the reactants.

callouts.p: A reaction is exothermic if more heat energy is released in forming bonds in the products than is required in breaking bonds in the reactants.

core.p: A reaction is **endothermic overall** when **less heat energy is released forming new bonds in the products than is needed to break the bonds in the reactants**. The reaction must take in the shortfall from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
bullets: Energy taken in (breaking bonds) > energy released (making bonds).
The overall energy change, ΔH, is **positive**.
The products are at a **higher energy** than the reactants.
Examples: thermal decomposition reactions (e.g. of calcium carbonate), dissolving ammonium nitrate in water, photosynthesis.
The products usually have weaker (or fewer) bonds overall than the reactants.

callouts.p: A reaction is endothermic if less heat energy is released in forming bonds in the products than is required in breaking bonds in the reactants.
