core.p: A **bond energy** is the amount of energy needed to break **one mole** of a particular covalent bond, measured in **kJ mol-1**. Exactly the same amount of energy is released when one mole of that bond is formed. Bond energies are always quoted as positive numbers and are given to you in a data table in the exam - you never need to memorise them.
bullets: Unit: **kJ mol-1** (kilojoules per mole).
Bigger bond energy = stronger bond = more energy to break and more energy released when formed.
Multiple bonds have larger bond energies: C=O (about 805) is much stronger than C-O (about 358).
The values are **average** bond energies, so calculated answers are approximate and may differ slightly from measured values.
You must use the value for the correct bond type - C=O and C-O are different bonds with different energies.

callouts.p: Always use the bond energy values printed in the question. They may differ slightly from those in this table, and the mark scheme is based on the printed data.

core.h: The bond energy calculation method (Higher tier)
core.p: To calculate the overall energy change of a reaction from bond energies, add up all the energy needed to break every bond in the reactants, add up all the energy released by making every bond in the products, then subtract.
bullets: Step 1: Write the **balanced equation** and draw (or picture) **displayed formulae** so every bond is visible.
Step 2: Count **every bond** in the reactants, remembering the balancing numbers (e.g. 2O2 means 2 O=O bonds).
Step 3: Energy in = sum of (number of bonds x bond energy) for the reactants.
Step 4: Count every bond in the products and work out energy out in the same way.
Step 5: **Energy change = energy in (bonds broken) - energy out (bonds made)**.
Step 6: Give the sign and units, e.g. -183 kJ mol-1. A negative answer means exothermic; positive means endothermic.

callouts.p: Energy change (ΔH) = total energy needed to break bonds in reactants - total energy released making bonds in products.
It is always bonds broken MINUS bonds made. Doing it the other way gives the right number with the wrong sign, which loses the final mark.

core.h: Worked energy diagram: hydrogen and chlorine
core.p: The reaction H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl shows the whole idea in one picture. Breaking 1 mol of H-H (436 kJ) and 1 mol of Cl-Cl (243 kJ) takes in 679 kJ. Making 2 mol of H-Cl (2 x 431 = 862 kJ) releases 862 kJ. More is released than taken in, so the reaction is exothermic.
bullets: Energy in = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ.
Energy out = 2 x 431 = 862 kJ.
On the diagram the 'atoms' level sits highest, because all bonds have been broken.
The products line is below the reactants line, which is the signature of an exothermic reaction.

callouts.p: Write 'bonds broken = ...' and 'bonds made = ...' separately. Even if you make an arithmetic slip, you can still pick up method marks.

core.p: Most lost marks in bond energy questions come from **miscounting bonds**, not from the subtraction. Drawing out displayed formulae makes the counting reliable.
bullets: CH4 has **4** C-H bonds.
CO2 has **2** C=O double bonds (O=C=O) - not 2 C-O bonds.
H2O has **2** O-H bonds, so 2H2O has **4** O-H bonds.
O2 has **1** O=O double bond; 3O2 means 3 O=O bonds.
NH3 has **3** N-H bonds, so 2NH3 contains 6 N-H bonds.
N2 contains one N≡N triple bond.
Multiply each bond by the **balancing number** in front of the formula before adding.

callouts.p: Forgetting to multiply by the balancing number (for example using 1 O=O instead of 2 for CH4 + 2O2) is the most common single error.

core.h: Calculating ΔH for the combustion of methane
core.p: Combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, is a classic exam calculation. It is strongly exothermic because the C=O and O-H bonds formed release much more energy than is needed to break the C-H and O=O bonds.
bullets: Bonds broken: 4 C-H = 4 x 413 = 1652; 2 O=O = 2 x 498 = 996; total = **2648 kJ**.
ΔH = 2648 - 3466 = **-818 kJ mol-1** (exothermic).
This large negative value is why methane is a useful fuel - lots of energy is transferred to the surroundings per mole burned.

callouts.p: Fuels release energy because the bonds made in CO2 and H2O are stronger overall than the bonds broken in the fuel and oxygen.

core.h: Working backwards: finding an unknown bond energy
core.p: Higher tier questions sometimes give you the overall energy change and ask you to find one missing bond energy. Use the same equation and rearrange it.
bullets: Write ΔH = bonds broken - bonds made, with the unknown bond as x.
Substitute all the known values, keeping signs carefully (an exothermic ΔH is negative).
Solve for x, then divide by the number of those bonds if there is more than one.
Check the answer is sensible: bond energies are positive and usually between about 150 and 1000 kJ mol-1.

callouts.p: If you get a negative bond energy, you have mixed up the sign of ΔH or the order of subtraction.

core.h: Why calculated values differ from measured values
core.p: Values calculated from bond energies often do not exactly match values measured in experiments. Understanding why earns marks in evaluation questions.
bullets: Bond energy tables give **average** values; the actual strength of a bond (e.g. C-H) varies slightly depending on the rest of the molecule.
Bond energies apply to substances in the **gas** state; in real reactions water might be a liquid, which releases extra energy.
In experiments, heat is lost to the surroundings, so measured temperature changes are usually smaller than expected.
Despite this, bond energy calculations correctly predict whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic and give a good estimate of the size.

callouts.p: The energy needed to start breaking bonds is linked to the activation energy, but activation energy is not the same as the total bond energy of the reactants.

analogy.p: Imagine you must pay £1 to pull apart each LEGO join in a model (breaking bonds costs energy) and you are paid £1 for each new join you click together, with stronger joins costing and paying more. If you earn more from building the new model than you paid to dismantle the old one, you make a profit - that is an exothermic reaction, and the profit is the energy given to the surroundings. If dismantling cost more than you earned building, you are out of pocket and must borrow from outside - that is endothermic. Where it breaks down: in real reactions bonds do not all break first and then all reform; breaking and making overlap, and the 'money' is energy transferred as heat, not something stored in the bond like a coin.

terms.d: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms, held by the electrostatic attraction between the shared electrons and both nuclei.
An endothermic process in which energy is taken in from the surroundings to separate bonded atoms.
An exothermic process in which energy is released to the surroundings as atoms form a bond.
A process or reaction that takes in heat energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
A process or reaction that gives out heat energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
The energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond, equal to the energy released when one mole of that bond forms; measured in kJ mol-1.
Kilojoules per mole: the unit for bond energies and for the overall energy change of a reaction.
Overall heat energy change of a reaction: energy needed to break bonds minus energy released making bonds.
Indicates an exothermic reaction: more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking bonds.
Indicates an endothermic reaction: more energy is taken in breaking bonds than is released making bonds.
A formula showing every atom and every bond as a line, used to count bonds accurately.
Two shared pairs of electrons between two atoms, e.g. O=O or C=O; stronger than the single bond between the same atoms.
Three shared pairs of electrons between two atoms, e.g. N≡N; very strong with a high bond energy.
A mean value for a bond type taken across many different compounds, which is why calculated energy changes are approximate.
Everything other than the reacting chemicals, such as the solvent, container and air, which gain or lose heat energy.

mistakes.w: Breaking bonds releases energy.
mistakes.r: Breaking bonds is endothermic: it takes in (requires) energy. Making bonds releases energy.

mistakes.w: Energy change = bonds made - bonds broken.
mistakes.r: Energy change = energy taken in breaking bonds - energy released making bonds (broken minus made).

mistakes.w: CO2 contains two C-O single bonds.
mistakes.r: CO2 is O=C=O: two C=O double bonds, so use the C=O bond energy twice.

mistakes.w: Using one O=O bond for CH4 + 2O2.
mistakes.r: Multiply by the balancing number: 2O2 contains 2 O=O bonds.

mistakes.w: Answer: 818 kJ (no sign).
mistakes.r: Give the sign and unit: -818 kJ mol-1, and state exothermic if asked.

mistakes.w: An exothermic reaction is one where the bonds broken are stronger.
mistakes.r: Exothermic means more energy is released forming bonds in the products than is needed to break bonds in the reactants.

mistakes.w: Endothermic reactions give out less heat so the temperature rises slightly.
mistakes.r: Endothermic reactions take in heat energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.

mistakes.w: H2O has one O-H bond.
mistakes.r: H2O is H-O-H with two O-H bonds; 2H2O has four O-H bonds.

exam.q: State whether bond breaking is an exothermic or endothermic process.
model: Endothermic.
exam.tip: One word answer - do not hedge with both terms.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of bonds, why the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen is exothermic.
model: More energy is released when bonds are made/formed in the products (water)
than is needed/taken in to break the bonds in the reactants (hydrogen and oxygen).
exam.tip: Use the comparison 'more...than' and say which bonds belong to reactants and which to products.

exam.q: Explain why some reactions are endothermic.
model: The energy needed to break bonds in the reactants
is greater than the energy released when new bonds form in the products.
exam.tip: Mirror image of the exothermic answer - keep the reactant/product link clear.

exam.q: Give the unit used for bond energies.
model: kJ mol-1 (kJ/mol).
exam.tip: kJ alone is not enough.

exam.q: Hydrogen reacts with chlorine: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ mol-1): H-H 436, Cl-Cl 243, H-Cl 431. Calculate the energy change for this reaction.
model: Energy to break bonds = 436 + 243 = 679 (kJ)
Energy released making bonds = 2 x 431 = 862 (kJ)
Energy change = 679 - 862 = -183 kJ mol-1
exam.tip: Remember there are TWO H-Cl bonds because of the 2 in front of HCl.

exam.q: Methane burns: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. Bond energies (kJ mol-1): C-H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O-H 464. Calculate the energy change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
model: Bonds broken = (4 x 413) + (2 x 498) = 2648 (kJ)
Energy change = 2648 - 3466 = -818 kJ mol-1
Exothermic because the energy change is negative / more energy released than taken in
exam.tip: Draw displayed formulae next to the equation and tick off each bond as you count it.

exam.q: The energy change for N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 is -93 kJ mol-1. Bond energies (kJ mol-1): N≡N 945, H-H 436. Calculate the bond energy of an N-H bond.
model: Bonds broken = 945 + (3 x 436) = 2253 (kJ)
exam.tip: 2NH3 contains 6 N-H bonds - divide by 6 at the end.

exam.q: Hydrogen bromide decomposes: 2HBr -> H2 + Br2. Bond energies (kJ mol-1): H-Br 366, H-H 436, Br-Br 193. Calculate the energy change and explain what the sign tells you.
model: Bonds broken = 2 x 366 = 732 (kJ)
Bonds made = 436 + 193 = 629 (kJ)
Energy change = 732 - 629 = +103 kJ mol-1
Positive so endothermic: more energy taken in breaking bonds than released making bonds
exam.tip: A positive answer is fine - do not assume every reaction is exothermic.

exam.q: Suggest why the energy change calculated from bond energies is different from the value measured in an experiment.
model: Bond energies are average values (taken from many compounds)
Heat is lost to the surroundings in the experiment / substances may not be gases
exam.tip: Average values is the key phrase examiners look for.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, how the energy changes in a chemical reaction decide whether it is exothermic or endothermic. Use the reaction of hydrogen with chlorine as an example.
model: Breaking bonds in the reactants is endothermic / requires energy
Making bonds in the products is exothermic / releases energy
If more energy is released making bonds than is needed to break bonds the reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative)
If less energy is released making bonds than is needed to break bonds the reaction is endothermic (ΔH positive)
For H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, breaking H-H and Cl-Cl takes in 679 kJ
Making 2 H-Cl bonds releases 862 kJ, so overall -183 kJ mol-1, exothermic; temperature of surroundings rises
exam.tip: Structure your answer: breaking, making, comparison for exothermic, comparison for endothermic, then the worked example.

worked.q: Calculate the energy change for the combustion of hydrogen: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Bond energies (kJ mol-1): H-H 436, O=O 498, O-H 464.
steps: Bonds broken: 2 H-H = 2 x 436 = 872 kJ; 1 O=O = 498 kJ.
Total energy in = 872 + 498 = 1370 kJ.
Bonds made: each H-O-H has 2 O-H bonds, so 2H2O has 4 O-H = 4 x 464 = 1856 kJ.
Energy change = bonds broken - bonds made = 1370 - 1856 = -486 kJ.
Negative, so the reaction is exothermic.
worked.ans: -486 kJ mol-1 (exothermic)

worked.q: Calculate the energy change for the Haber process reaction N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. Bond energies (kJ mol-1): N≡N 945, H-H 436, N-H 391.
steps: Bonds broken: 1 N≡N = 945 kJ; 3 H-H = 3 x 436 = 1308 kJ.
Total energy in = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ.
Bonds made: each NH3 has 3 N-H bonds, so 2NH3 has 6 N-H = 6 x 391 = 2346 kJ.
Energy change = 2253 - 2346 = -93 kJ.
Negative, so exothermic.
worked.ans: -93 kJ mol-1 (exothermic)

worked.q: For H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl the energy change is -184 kJ mol-1. H-H = 436 kJ mol-1 and Cl-Cl = 242 kJ mol-1. Calculate the H-Cl bond energy.
steps: ΔH = bonds broken - bonds made.
Bonds broken = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ.
-184 = 678 - 2x, where x is the H-Cl bond energy.
worked.ans: H-Cl bond energy = 431 kJ mol-1

chem_edx.7.8.summary: A **reaction profile** is a diagram showing how the energy of the reacting substances changes as a reaction proceeds, from reactants, over an energy 'hump', down (or up) to products. The height of the hump above the reactants is the **activation energy**: the **minimum energy that particles must have when they collide in order to react**. You must be able to draw and fully label reaction profiles for both **exothermic** reactions (products lower than reactants) and **endothermic** reactions (products higher than reactants), showing the activation energy and the overall energy change.

core.p: A **reaction profile** (also called an energy profile) is a graph with **energy** on the vertical axis and **progress of reaction** on the horizontal axis. It shows the energy stored in the reactants at the start, the energy barrier that has to be overcome, and the energy stored in the products at the end.
bullets: Vertical axis: **energy** (sometimes 'energy / kJ'). Horizontal axis: **progress of reaction** (sometimes 'reaction pathway').
A horizontal line on the left shows the **energy of the reactants**.
A curve rises to a peak (the energy barrier) and then falls.
A horizontal line on the right shows the **energy of the products**.
The height difference between the reactant and product lines is the **overall energy change**.
The height from the reactant line to the top of the hump is the **activation energy**.

callouts.p: The horizontal axis is progress of reaction, NOT time. Do not label it 'time'.

core.p: Particles must collide to react, but not every collision works. Only collisions with **enough energy** lead to a reaction. That minimum amount of energy is the **activation energy**. It is the 'energy barrier' that must be climbed before the reaction can happen.
bullets: Activation energy is the **minimum energy** needed for a reaction to occur when particles collide.
Collisions with energy **less than** the activation energy do not produce a reaction - the particles just bounce apart.
Collisions with energy **equal to or greater than** the activation energy are **successful collisions** and produce products.
Every reaction has an activation energy, whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
The activation energy is always drawn as an **upward** arrow from the reactant level to the peak of the curve.

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy needed for a reaction to occur / for colliding particles to react.
Say MINIMUM energy. 'The energy needed to start a reaction' on its own may not get the mark.

core.p: To make new bonds, some of the existing bonds in the reactants must **start to break** first. Breaking bonds requires energy (it is endothermic), so the colliding particles must bring enough energy to get the process started. Once the reaction is under way, energy released by making new bonds can supply the activation energy for further particles in an exothermic reaction.
bullets: The energy hump represents the energy needed to begin breaking bonds in the reactants.
Particles get this energy from their **kinetic energy** when they collide.
A **high activation energy** means few collisions are energetic enough, so the reaction is slow or does not start at room temperature.
A **low activation energy** means many collisions succeed, so the reaction is fast.
Heating gives particles more energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have at least the activation energy.

callouts.p: Activation energy is the bridge between energy changes and collision theory: rate depends on how many collisions per second have at least the activation energy.

core.h: Why some exothermic reactions need a 'kick start'
core.p: Many exothermic reactions do not happen on their own even though they release lots of energy overall. This is because of the activation energy barrier. A spark, a flame or heating supplies enough energy to the first particles; after that, the energy released keeps the reaction going.
bullets: Methane (natural gas) does not burn in air until a **spark or flame** supplies the activation energy.
A match must be **struck** to provide energy through friction before it lights.
Magnesium ribbon must be **heated** in a Bunsen flame before it burns brightly.
Once started, the energy released by these exothermic reactions supplies the activation energy for more particles, so the reaction is self-sustaining.
Endothermic reactions need a continuous energy supply: they need the activation energy and also take in energy overall.

callouts.p: If asked why a fuel needs a spark, say the spark provides the activation energy (the minimum energy needed for the reaction to start).

core.h: Reaction profile for an exothermic reaction
core.p: In an **exothermic** reaction, energy is transferred **to the surroundings**, so the products end up with **less energy than the reactants**. On the profile, the product line is **lower** than the reactant line.
bullets: Reactant line on the left, **higher** than the product line on the right.
A hump rises above the reactant line - its height above the reactants is the activation energy.
The **overall energy change** arrow points **downwards** from the reactant level to the product level.
The energy change is **negative** (ΔH is negative) because energy is given out.
Examples: combustion, neutralisation, respiration, many oxidation reactions.

callouts.p: Products lower than reactants; energy change arrow points down; energy given out to surroundings.

fig.cap: Reaction profile for an exothermic reaction. The activation energy (Ea) is measured from the reactant level up to the peak. The products are lower than the reactants, so the overall energy change (ΔH) is negative and energy is given out to the surroundings.

core.h: Reaction profile for an endothermic reaction
core.p: In an **endothermic** reaction, energy is taken in **from the surroundings**, so the products end up with **more energy than the reactants**. On the profile, the product line is **higher** than the reactant line.
bullets: Reactant line on the left, **lower** than the product line on the right.
The hump is still drawn above both lines - the activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak.
The **overall energy change** arrow points **upwards** from the reactant level to the product level.
The energy change is **positive** (ΔH is positive) because energy is taken in.
In an endothermic reaction the activation energy is always **larger** than the overall energy change, because the peak is above the products.
Examples: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate, the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate.

callouts.p: Products higher than reactants; energy change arrow points up; energy taken in from surroundings.

core.h: How to draw and label a profile in the exam
core.p: Reaction profile drawing questions are marked on specific features. Make each one clear and use ruled lines for levels and arrows.
bullets: Label the axes: **energy** (vertical) and **progress of reaction** (horizontal).
Draw and label a horizontal **reactants** line and a horizontal **products** line at the correct relative heights.
Draw a smooth curve joining them that rises to a single peak **above both** lines.
Draw an arrow from the **reactant line** to the **peak** and label it **activation energy**.
Draw an arrow from the **reactant line** to the **product line** and label it **overall energy change** (or ΔH).
Check the direction: arrows start at the reactants. Activation energy always points up; the energy change points down for exothermic and up for endothermic.
You may write the formulae of the reactants and products on the lines (e.g. CH4 + 2O2 and CO2 + 2H2O).

callouts.p: The activation energy arrow must start at the REACTANT level, not at the products or the x-axis. Double-headed arrows are usually accepted for the size, but must run between the correct levels.

fig.cap: Reaction profile for an endothermic reaction. The products are higher than the reactants, so the overall energy change (ΔH) is positive and energy is taken in from the surroundings. Ea is still measured from the reactants to the peak.

core.p: Profiles in exams often have energy values marked on the axis, or letters A, B, C on arrows. You need to identify which arrow is which and calculate sizes.
bullets: **Activation energy = energy at peak - energy of reactants.**
**Overall energy change = energy of products - energy of reactants.** A negative answer means exothermic; positive means endothermic.
An arrow from the **products** to the peak is NOT the activation energy of the forward reaction.
An arrow from the axis (zero) to the reactant line just shows the energy of the reactants, not an energy change.
Always include units, usually kJ or kJ mol-1.

callouts.p: When given labelled arrows, find the one that starts at the reactants and ends at the top of the hump - that is the activation energy.

core.h: Linking profiles to bond breaking and making
core.p: The shape of a reaction profile connects to what is happening to the bonds. Going up the hump, bonds in the reactants are starting to break, which needs energy. Coming down the other side, new bonds are forming in the products, which releases energy.
bullets: Rising part of the curve: energy taken in as reactant bonds begin to break (endothermic).
Falling part of the curve: energy released as product bonds form (exothermic).
Exothermic overall: more energy released making bonds than taken in breaking bonds, so products end lower.
Endothermic overall: less energy released making bonds than taken in breaking bonds, so products end higher.
The activation energy is not the same as the total bond energy of the reactants; bonds do not all have to break completely before new ones start to form.

core.p: A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction by providing an **alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy**. On a reaction profile this is shown as a **lower hump** between the same reactant and product lines. Catalysts are covered in detail in points 7.6-7.7, but profile questions often combine the two ideas.
bullets: Catalysed profile: same reactants level, same products level, lower peak.
The **overall energy change is unchanged** by a catalyst because the reactants and products are the same.
With a lower activation energy, a greater proportion of collisions are successful, so the rate increases.

callouts.p: A catalyst does NOT change the energy of the reactants or products, so do not move the levels when drawing the catalysed curve.

core.h: Comparing activation energies of different reactions
core.p: Reactions differ hugely in their activation energies, and this explains much everyday chemistry. The size of the activation energy is unrelated to whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
bullets: Very low activation energy: reactions happen instantly at room temperature, e.g. neutralisation of an acid by an alkali or precipitation reactions.
High activation energy: reactions need heating or a spark to start, e.g. combustion of fuels.
A reaction can be very exothermic yet have a high activation energy (e.g. burning petrol), which is why fuels can be stored safely.
A larger activation energy means a slower reaction at a given temperature.

callouts.p: The size of the activation energy and the size/sign of the overall energy change are separate: one is about getting started, the other about the overall energy difference.

analogy.t: Pushing a boulder over a hill
analogy.p: Think of the reactants as a boulder sitting in a valley on one side of a hill. To get it into the valley on the other side (the products), you must first push it up to the top of the hill: the height of the hill above the starting valley is the activation energy. If the far valley is lower than the starting valley, the boulder ends up lower and energy is released overall - exothermic. If the far valley is higher, you have put in more energy than you get back - endothermic. A small push (not enough energy) just makes the boulder roll back, like a collision with too little energy. Where it breaks down: a real reaction involves billions of particles colliding randomly, each with different energies, not one boulder; and the energy is transferred as heat to and from the surroundings rather than as height.

terms.d: A diagram of energy against progress of reaction showing the energy of reactants, products and the activation energy barrier.
The minimum amount of energy needed for a reaction to occur when particles collide.
The horizontal axis of a reaction profile, showing the change from reactants to products (not time).
A collision between particles with energy at least equal to the activation energy, which results in a reaction.
A reaction that transfers heat energy to the surroundings; products have less energy than reactants and the energy change is negative.
A reaction that takes in heat energy from the surroundings; products have more energy than reactants and the energy change is positive.
The difference in energy between products and reactants: energy of products minus energy of reactants.
The hump on a reaction profile that particles must overcome; its height above the reactants is the activation energy.
The starting substances in a reaction, shown as the left-hand horizontal line on a profile.
The substances formed in a reaction, shown as the right-hand horizontal line on a profile.
Everything other than the reacting chemicals, e.g. the solvent, container and air.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, by providing a pathway with lower activation energy.
Energy of movement; colliding particles must have enough to meet the activation energy.
An endothermic process needed to start a reaction, linked to the rising part of the profile.

mistakes.w: Activation energy is the energy given out by a reaction.
mistakes.r: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur (for colliding particles to react).

mistakes.w: Drawing the activation energy arrow from the x-axis to the peak.
mistakes.r: The activation energy arrow goes from the reactant energy level to the top of the curve.

mistakes.w: Labelling the horizontal axis 'time'.
mistakes.r: Label it 'progress of reaction'.

mistakes.w: Exothermic profile drawn with products higher than reactants.
mistakes.r: In an exothermic reaction products are lower than reactants because energy is given out.

mistakes.w: Drawing the energy change arrow from products to reactants for an exothermic reaction.
mistakes.r: Draw the overall energy change arrow from the reactant level to the product level (pointing down for exothermic).

mistakes.w: Endothermic reactions don't have an activation energy because they take in energy anyway.
mistakes.r: Every reaction has an activation energy; on an endothermic profile the peak is still above the products.

mistakes.w: A catalyst lowers the energy of the products, so more energy is released.
mistakes.r: A catalyst lowers the activation energy only; the overall energy change is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Ea = peak energy - product energy.
mistakes.r: Ea for the reaction = peak energy - reactant energy.

exam.q: What is meant by the term activation energy?
model: The minimum (amount of) energy needed for a reaction to occur / for particles to react when they collide.
exam.tip: The word minimum is what examiners look for.

exam.q: Explain why a mixture of methane and air does not react until a spark is applied.
model: The spark provides the activation energy
Particles do not have enough energy at room temperature to react when they collide / collisions are not successful
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'provides the activation energy'.

exam.q: On a reaction profile, state what is plotted on each axis.
model: Vertical axis: energy
Horizontal axis: progress of reaction
exam.tip: Not time - this is a frequent lost mark.

exam.q: Describe how the reaction profile for an exothermic reaction differs from that for an endothermic reaction.
model: Exothermic: products at a lower energy than reactants
Endothermic: products at a higher energy than reactants
exam.tip: Compare both reactions explicitly using 'lower' and 'higher'.

exam.q: Draw a reaction profile for the combustion of methane, an exothermic reaction. Label the activation energy and the overall energy change.
model: Reactants line higher than products line, both labelled (e.g. CH4 + 2O2 and CO2 + 2H2O)
Curve rising to a peak above the reactants and falling to the products
Activation energy shown by an arrow from reactants level to the peak
Overall energy change shown by an arrow from reactants level down to products level
exam.tip: Label the axes too even if the question gives a frame - it costs nothing.

exam.q: Draw a reaction profile for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, an endothermic reaction. Label the activation energy and the energy change.
model: Products (CaO + CO2) higher than reactants (CaCO3)
Activation energy arrow from reactants up to the peak
Energy change arrow from reactants up to products
exam.tip: In an endothermic profile the energy change arrow points upwards.

exam.q: On a reaction profile the reactants are at 120 kJ, the peak is at 290 kJ and the products are at 40 kJ. Calculate the activation energy and the overall energy change.
model: Activation energy = 290 - 120 = 170 kJ
Energy change = 40 - 120 = -80 kJ
Exothermic (because negative / products lower)
exam.tip: Always subtract the reactant value: peak minus reactants, products minus reactants.

exam.q: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the number of successful collisions in a reaction.
model: Particles gain more (kinetic) energy
A greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
exam.tip: Link the energy of the particles to the activation energy.

exam.q: Explain why, for an endothermic reaction, the activation energy must be greater than the overall energy change.
model: The products are at a higher energy than the reactants
The peak of the curve must be above the products, so the distance from reactants to peak is bigger than reactants to products
exam.tip: Think about the drawing - the hump must sit above both lines.

exam.q: Compare the reaction profiles of an exothermic reaction and an endothermic reaction. In your answer refer to activation energy, the energy of reactants and products, and energy transfer to or from the surroundings.
model: Both profiles have energy on the y-axis and progress of reaction on the x-axis
Both have an activation energy: minimum energy for reaction, shown from reactants to the peak
Exothermic: products lower in energy than reactants; energy given out to surroundings
Exothermic: energy change is negative, temperature of surroundings increases
Endothermic: products higher in energy than reactants; energy taken in from surroundings
Endothermic: energy change is positive, temperature of surroundings decreases; activation energy larger than the energy change
exam.tip: Organise into 'similarities' then 'differences' so the examiner can tick each point.

worked.q: A reaction profile shows reactants at 50 kJ mol-1, a peak at 230 kJ mol-1 and products at 140 kJ mol-1. Find the activation energy and energy change, and state the type of reaction.
steps: Activation energy = peak - reactants = 230 - 50 = 180 kJ mol-1.
Energy change = products - reactants = 140 - 50 = +90 kJ mol-1.
The energy change is positive and the products are higher than the reactants.
So energy is taken in from the surroundings: endothermic.
worked.ans: Ea = 180 kJ mol-1; energy change = +90 kJ mol-1; endothermic

worked.q: A student says: 'Burning wood is exothermic, so it should start on its own without needing a match.' Write a model answer correcting this.
steps: State the key idea: all reactions have an activation energy.
Define it: the minimum energy needed for particles to react when they collide.
At room temperature, too few collisions between wood and oxygen particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
The match flame supplies the activation energy to start the reaction.
Once burning, the energy released by the exothermic reaction provides the activation energy for further reaction, so it keeps going.
worked.ans: Being exothermic does not mean a reaction starts by itself; the match provides the activation energy, after which the energy released keeps the reaction going.

worked.q: A profile is labelled with arrows: P from reactants to peak, Q from products to peak, R from reactants down to products. Identify the activation energy and the energy change, and say whether the reaction is exothermic.
steps: The activation energy starts at the reactants and ends at the peak, so it is P.
The overall energy change runs from reactants to products, so it is R.
R points down, meaning the products are lower in energy than the reactants.
So energy is given out to the surroundings.
worked.ans: P = activation energy; R = overall energy change; exothermic
